statement: The microservices pattern language is organised into three groups of patterns: application patterns, application infrastructure patterns, and infrastructure patterns.
Each entry in the pattern language is presented as a motivating problem paired with one or more solution patterns, and solutions may be related as general-versus-specific or as alternative options.
Decompose by business capability and decompose by subdomain are the application-decomposition patterns for splitting an application into services.
Service per team and self-contained service are decomposition patterns that align service boundaries to teams and to service autonomy.
The Saga pattern maintains data consistency for a business transaction that spans multiple services.
Database per service and shared database are the two alternative data-architecture patterns for how a service owns its data.
Event sourcing and domain event are event-based data patterns for persisting and propagating state changes.
API composition and CQRS are the query patterns for retrieving data that spans multiple services.
The transactional outbox pattern, drained by transaction log tailing or a polling publisher, publishes messages reliably as part of a database transaction.
Consumer-driven contract test, consumer-side contract test, and service component test are the microservice testing patterns.
Server-side page fragment composition and client-side UI composition are the UI patterns for assembling a user interface from multiple services.
Microservice chassis, service template, and externalised configuration are the cross-cutting-concern patterns for services.
The Access Token pattern conveys the caller's identity and authorisation between services.
The observability patterns are health check API, log aggregation, distributed tracing, application metrics, exception tracking, audit logging, and log deployments and changes.
The Circuit Breaker pattern is the reliability pattern for handling partial failure of inter-service calls.
Remote procedure invocation and messaging are the two inter-service communication-style patterns.
The service-deployment patterns are multiple services per host, single service per host, service-per-VM, service-per-container, serverless deployment, and a service deployment platform.
The service-discovery patterns are client-side discovery, server-side discovery, service registry, self registration, and third-party registration.
API gateway and backends for frontends are the external-API patterns that expose services to outside clients.
Sidecar and service mesh are the communication-infrastructure patterns for handling inter-service communication concerns out of process.
A pattern is a reusable solution to a problem that recurs within a particular context.
A well-formed pattern description states not only the benefits of a solution but also its drawbacks and the issues that must be resolved to implement it successfully.
Objectively weighing a solution's drawbacks alongside its benefits leads to better architectural decision-making.

Adopting microservices is a means to an end (fast, reliable, frequent software delivery), not a goal in itself, so a team should understand the architecture's benefits, drawbacks, and when to use it before adopting it.
The monolithic architecture structures an application as a single executable or deployable component (for example a single WAR/JAR, executable, or source-tree hierarchy).
The monolithic architecture is not inherently bad and is a sound choice for a small, simple application.
condition: the application is still small and simple

statement: For a small application, the monolithic architecture is simple to develop, easy to change radically, straightforward to test end-to-end, straightforward to deploy, and easy to scale by running multiple instances behind a load balancer.
Successful applications tend to outgrow the monolithic architecture as both the codebase and the development team steadily grow.
Once a monolith grows too large for any single developer to fully understand, fixing bugs and correctly implementing new features become slow and error-prone, causing missed deadlines.
condition: the monolith has grown beyond comprehension of a single developer

statement: Excessive monolith complexity becomes a downward spiral: each change made without full understanding adds complexity and further erodes the intended modular architecture toward a big ball of mud.

A large monolithic codebase slows the development feedback loop by overloading the IDE and lengthening build and application-startup times, which degrades the edit-build-run-test cycle and developer productivity.
In monolithic hell the path from code commit to production is long and arduous, with infrequent, painful, and often manual deployments.

In a hexagonal architecture the business logic forms the core, surrounded by adapters: inbound adapters handle requests by invoking the business logic, while outbound adapters let the business logic access the database and invoke external/cloud services.

A monolith is hard to scale when its modules have conflicting resource requirements (e.g. memory-intensive vs CPU-intensive), because all modules share one deployable and force a compromise on server configuration.
A monolith has poor fault isolation because all modules run in one process, so a single module's fault (e.g. a memory leak) can crash every instance of the application.
A monolith tends to lock a team into an increasingly obsolete technology stack, because rewriting the whole application to adopt a new language or framework is expensive and risky.

Software architecture has little to do with functional requirements: any architecture can implement a given set of use cases, so an architecture must be evaluated by its effect on quality-of-service (nonfunctional) attributes rather than by features.
As a monolith grows, the quality attributes that suffer most are those governing delivery velocity: maintainability, extensibility, and testability.

A disciplined team can only slow the descent into monolithic hell (by preserving modularity and writing comprehensive automated tests); it cannot escape the problems of a large team on one monolith or an obsolete stack, so migrating architecture is eventually necessary.
For a large, complex application, teams should consider adopting the microservice architecture.
condition: the application is large and complex

statement: The microservice architecture is an architectural style that functionally decomposes an application into a set of services; its definition says nothing about size.
A service should not be defined by size metrics such as lines of code or development time; what matters is that each service has a focused, cohesive set of responsibilities.
The scale cube defines three independent ways to scale an application: X-axis (horizontal duplication), Y-axis (functional decomposition), and Z-axis (data partitioning).
X-axis scaling runs N identical instances behind a load balancer that distributes requests among them, improving an application's capacity and availability.

Z-axis scaling runs multiple identical instances where a router uses a request attribute (e.g. userId) to route each request, so each instance owns only a subset of the data; it scales increasing transaction and data volumes.

Only Y-axis scaling (functional decomposition into services) addresses growing development and application complexity; X- and Z-axis scaling improve capacity and availability but do not reduce complexity.
A service is a mini-application implementing narrowly focused, cohesive functionality, and each service is itself scaled with X-axis cloning and possibly Z-axis partitioning.
In a monolith, module boundaries defined only by language constructs (packages) and build artifacts (JARs) are easily bypassed, so long-lived monoliths degenerate into big balls of mud.

The microservice architecture uses the service as the unit of modularity; a service's API is an impermeable boundary that cannot be bypassed to access internal classes, which preserves modularity over time.

Each service should own its private datastore and services should communicate only via APIs; this loose coupling lets teams change a service's schema without cross-team coordination and isolates services at runtime (one service is never blocked by another holding a database lock).
exception: owning a database does not require owning a separate database server; databases may be logically separated on shared infrastructure

statement: Microservices differ from SOA on three axes: inter-service communication (SOA uses smart pipes/ESB and heavyweight protocols like SOAP/WS*, microservices use dumb pipes such as message brokers or lightweight REST/gRPC), data (SOA shares a global data model and databases, microservices use a database and domain model per service), and service size (SOA integrates a few large services, microservices are many smaller services).

The most important benefit of the microservice architecture is that it enables continuous delivery and deployment of large, complex applications, through the testability, independent deployability, and team autonomy that small, independently deployable services provide.

Because each service is relatively small, it is easier for a developer to understand, does not slow the IDE, and starts faster than a large monolith, which raises developer productivity and speeds deployments.

Each service can be scaled independently using X-axis cloning and Z-axis partitioning and deployed on hardware best suited to its resource requirements, unlike a monolith where components with conflicting resource needs must be deployed together.

The microservice architecture provides better fault isolation: a fault such as a memory leak in one service affects only that service while others keep serving requests, whereas one misbehaving component can bring down an entire monolith.

The microservice architecture eliminates long-term commitment to a single technology stack: developers can choose the best-suited language and frameworks per service, and small services are cheap enough to rewrite that a failed technology trial can be discarded without risking the whole project.

There is no concrete, well-defined algorithm for decomposing a system into services; decomposing incorrectly produces a distributed monolith (coupled services that must be deployed together) that carries the drawbacks of both the monolithic and microservice architectures.

The microservice architecture forces developers to handle the complexity of a distributed system: services must use interprocess communication (more complex than a method call) and each service must be designed to tolerate partial failure when a remote service is unavailable or slow.

Because each service has its own database, implementing use cases that span services requires unfamiliar techniques: sagas to maintain data consistency across services, and API composition or CQRS views to implement queries that span services.

Successfully using microservices requires developers with sophisticated development and delivery skills, because IDEs and tools are focused on monoliths and writing automated tests that span services is challenging.

The microservice architecture introduces significant operational complexity from many more moving parts in production, so it requires a high level of deployment automation such as automated deployment tooling, a PaaS, or a container-orchestration platform like Kubernetes.

Deploying a feature that spans multiple services requires careful cross-team coordination and a rollout plan that orders service deployments by their dependencies, unlike a monolith where multiple components can be deployed atomically.

A startup or first-version application should almost certainly begin as a monolith, because it usually lacks the problems microservices solve and an elaborate distributed architecture slows the rapid iteration a young product needs.
condition: the application is new and the priority is rapidly evolving the business model

statement: An application should be functionally decomposed into microservices later, once the dominant problem becomes managing complexity rather than rapid iteration.
condition: managing complexity has become the dominant problem

statement: Advising to always use the microservice architecture is bad advice, and advising to never use it is equally bad advice; appropriateness depends on the application's context and many factors.
Technology should be described in the pattern format because it is objective: the format forces you to state the drawbacks of a solution, not just its benefits.

A pattern is valuable partly because it must describe the context in which it applies, since a solution that works at one scale (e.g. Netflix) may be the wrong approach for an application with far fewer users.
A well-structured pattern's Forces section lists the issues that must be addressed when solving the problem; forces can conflict, so which to prioritize depends on the context.

A pattern's Resulting Context section gives a less biased view for better decisions by describing three things: the benefits (resolved forces), the drawbacks (unresolved forces), and the new issues introduced by applying the pattern.
Patterns relate to one another through five relationship types: predecessor, successor, alternative, generalization, and specialization.

A pattern language for an architecture should first help decide whether to adopt the architecture (by describing the alternatives and their trade-offs) and then help apply it effectively by solving the issues it introduces.

The traditional approach of distributed transactions (two-phase commit / 2PC) is not a viable option for maintaining data consistency in a modern microservice application; the Saga pattern should be used instead.

Because a service's data is accessible only through its API, you cannot run distributed queries against its database; queries that span services must be implemented with either the API composition pattern (invoke service APIs and aggregate results) or the CQRS pattern (maintain queryable read replicas).

The traditional, often manual, language-specific packaging deployment (e.g. WAR files) does not scale to a microservice architecture; you should use a highly automated, self-service deployment platform based on VMs, containers, or serverless technology.

Diagnosing a microservice application is harder than a monolith because a single request bounces across multiple services with no single log file to examine, so observability must be designed in using patterns such as Health check API, Log aggregation, Distributed tracing, Exception tracking, Application metrics, and Audit logging.

While individual microservices are easier to test because they are smaller, teams must still verify services work together while avoiding complex, slow, and brittle end-to-end tests, using consumer-driven contract tests, consumer-side contract tests, and service component tests.

Rather than reimplementing cross-cutting concerns (observability, service discovery, externalized configuration) from scratch in each new service, teams should apply the Microservice Chassis pattern and build services on a framework that handles these concerns.

In a microservice architecture, users are typically authenticated once at the API gateway, which then passes user identity and roles to downstream services via the Access Token pattern (e.g. a JWT the services validate).

Rapid, frequent, and reliable delivery of a large, complex application requires the combination of DevOps (continuous delivery/deployment), small autonomous cross-functional teams, and the microservice architecture; the architecture alone is not sufficient.

Because team communication overhead grows on the order of O(N^2), a large single team should be refactored into a team of teams, each small (roughly 8-12 people) with a clearly defined business-oriented mission and cross-functional enough to develop, test, and deploy its services without frequent inter-team coordination.

By Conway's law an application's architecture mirrors the communication structure of the organization that built it, so teams should apply the reverse Conway maneuver: design the organization so its structure mirrors the intended microservice architecture, keeping teams as loosely coupled as the services.

A microservice organization scales by adding teams and by splitting a team together with its service(s) when it grows too large; because the teams are loosely coupled you can add people without the communication overhead that reduces a large team's productivity.

Using the microservice architecture with a waterfall process squanders most of its benefit; adopting microservices requires agile practices such as Scrum or Kanban and, ideally, continuous delivery/deployment as part of DevOps.

Continuous delivery is the ability to get all types of change (features, config changes, bug fixes, experiments) into production safely, quickly, and sustainably; its key characteristic is that the software is always releasable, which relies on a high level of automation including automated testing. Continuous deployment goes further by automatically deploying releasable code to production.

Four useful metrics for assessing software delivery are deployment frequency, lead time (check-in to deployed), mean time to recover from a production problem, and change failure rate (percentage of changes causing a production problem).

Adopting microservices changes people's working environment, so leaders must manage the emotional transition (ending/letting-go, then a confusing neutral zone, then a new beginning) or adoption will be a bumpy ride.

The software architecture of a system is the set of structures needed to reason about it: the software elements, the relations among them, and the properties of both; in essence it is the decomposition of the application into parts and the relationships between them.

Decomposition matters because it enables the division of labor and knowledge (letting multiple teams work productively) and defines how the software elements interact, and it is this decomposition and its relationships that determine the application's quality attributes.

An application's architecture is multidimensional and is best described with the 4+1 view model: the logical view (classes/packages developers create), the implementation view (build output: modules/JARs and components/WARs/executables), the process view (runtime processes and their interprocess communication), and the deployment view (processes mapped to machines and networking), plus scenarios that animate how elements collaborate.

Architecture matters because it determines the application's quality-of-service attributes (the -ilities): runtime qualities such as scalability and reliability, and development-time qualities such as maintainability, testability, and deployability.

An architectural style defines a family of systems by fixing the vocabulary of components and connectors that may be used and the constraints on how they combine; a real application typically uses a combination of architectural styles.

The layered (three-tier: presentation, business-logic, persistence) architecture has significant drawbacks: it assumes a single presentation layer and a single persistence layer, and it makes the business logic depend on persistence, which misrepresents real dependencies and hinders testing the business logic without a database.

The hexagonal architecture places the business logic at the center with inbound adapters that handle external requests by invoking an inbound port and outbound adapters that implement outbound ports to invoke external systems; its defining characteristic is that the business logic depends on nothing while the adapters depend on it.

In a hexagonal architecture a port defines a set of operations through which the business logic interacts with the outside (in Java, an interface): an inbound port is an API the business logic exposes (e.g. a service interface) and an outbound port is how the business logic invokes external systems (e.g. a repository interface).

The hexagonal architecture decouples the business logic from presentation and data-access logic, which makes the business logic easy to test in isolation and lets it be invoked by, and invoke, multiple adapters; it is a good way to describe the architecture of each service in a microservice architecture.

The monolithic architecture is an architectural style that structures the implementation view as a single component (a single executable or WAR); it says nothing about the other views, so a monolith may still organize its logical view as a hexagonal architecture.

The microservice architecture is an architectural style that structures the implementation view as multiple components (the services), whose connectors are the interprocess communication protocols that let the services collaborate.
A key constraint of the microservice architecture is that services are loosely coupled, which places restrictions on how the services may collaborate.

A service is a standalone, independently deployable software component that implements useful functionality and exposes an API composed of commands (which perform actions and update data), queries (which retrieve data), and events (which it publishes for clients to consume).
A service's API encapsulates its internal implementation and, unlike a monolith, cannot be bypassed by a developer, so the microservice architecture enforces the application's modularity.

Each service may have its own architecture and potentially its own technology stack, but a typical service uses a hexagonal architecture whose API is implemented by adapters that interact with the service's business logic.

Loose coupling means all interaction with a service happens through its API, which encapsulates its implementation, so the implementation can change without impacting clients; loosely coupled services are key to maintainability and testability.

Loose coupling prohibits services from communicating through a shared database: treat a service's persistent data like the private fields of a class, so a team can change its schema without coordinating with others and one service cannot hold database locks that block another.
exception: the trade-off is that maintaining data consistency and querying across services become more complex once databases are not shared

statement: Do not put functionality that is likely to change into a shared library used by multiple services, because a change would force all consuming services to be rebuilt and redeployed together, reintroducing coupling; implement likely-to-change functionality (e.g. Order management) as a service, and reserve shared libraries for functionality unlikely to change (e.g. a generic Money type).
The size of a service is not a useful design metric; a better goal is that a well-designed service can be developed by a small team with minimal lead time and minimal collaboration with other teams.

Signs that a service is wrongly defined: if it requires a large team or is slow to test it should be split; if it must constantly change because other services change (or triggers changes in them) it is not loosely coupled and may indicate a distributed monolith.

The primary goal of the microservice architecture is to improve development-time attributes (maintainability, testability, deployability) so an organization can develop better software faster; improved scalability is a secondary benefit, not the main goal.

Define an application's microservice architecture with a three-step, iterative (not mechanical) process: identify the system operations, decompose into services, and define each service's API and collaborations.

A system operation is a technology-agnostic abstraction of a request the application must handle: either a command that creates, updates, or deletes data, or a query that retrieves data; its behavior is defined against an abstract domain model, and system operations become the architectural scenarios that show how services collaborate.

Derive the high-level domain model primarily from the nouns of the user stories and the system operations primarily from the verbs; this early domain model is a deliberate simplification whose purpose is to provide the vocabulary for describing system operations, since each service will later own its own domain model.

Specify each command by its parameters, return value, and behavior expressed as preconditions (true when the operation is invoked) and post-conditions (true afterward); when invoked, the operation verifies the preconditions and performs the actions needed to make the post-conditions true.

There are four main obstacles to decomposing an application into services: network latency (a decomposition may cause too many round-trips), synchronous inter-service communication reducing availability, the need to maintain data consistency across services, and god classes used throughout the application.
Services should be organized around business concepts rather than technical concepts; every sound decomposition strategy results in business-oriented services.

The Decompose by business capability pattern defines services that correspond to business capabilities, where a business capability is something a business does to generate value (e.g. Order management, Inventory management).

Business capabilities are identified by analyzing the organization's purpose, structure, and business processes; a capability is often focused on a particular business object and can be decomposed into sub-capabilities.

Organizing services around business capabilities yields a relatively stable architecture, because capabilities capture what the business does (which is stable) rather than how it does it (which changes over time).

An initial service decomposition is only a first attempt and should be expected to evolve as the team learns the domain: services may be combined when a decomposition causes excessive interprocess communication, or split when a service grows too complex.

Domain-driven design (DDD) builds complex software around an object-oriented domain model that captures domain knowledge and defines the team's Ubiquitous Language, and this model is closely mirrored in the design and implementation.

Traditional enterprise modeling uses a single enterprise-wide model with one definition of each entity, which is hard to get agreement on, overly complex for any one part of the organization, and confusing because different parts use the same term for different concepts; DDD avoids this by defining multiple domain models, each with an explicit scope.

The Decompose by subdomain pattern defines a service per DDD subdomain: subdomains (parts of the problem space) are identified like business capabilities by analyzing areas of expertise, and each bounded context (the scope of a domain model plus the code that implements it) becomes a service or set of services.

DDD and the microservice architecture align closely: subdomains and bounded contexts map to services, autonomous teams owning services matches each domain model being owned by one team, and giving each subdomain its own domain model eliminates god classes.

Apply the Single Responsibility Principle (a class should have only one reason to change) at the service level: define small, cohesive services that each have a single responsibility, which reduces service size and increases stability.

Apply the Common Closure Principle at the service level: package components that change for the same reason into the same service so that a requirement change ideally affects only one team and one service; the Common Closure Principle is the antidote to the distributed monolith anti-pattern.

When a decomposition causes too many round-trips between two services (network latency), reduce it by implementing a batch API that fetches multiple objects in one round-trip, or, when that is insufficient, combine the services to replace expensive interprocess communication with local method calls.

Synchronous interprocess communication reduces availability: a service that synchronously invokes others (e.g. via REST) cannot complete its operation if any of them is unavailable, so asynchronous messaging, which removes tight coupling and improves availability, is often the better choice.

For operations that must atomically update data in multiple services, use a saga (a sequence of local transactions coordinated by messaging) rather than a two-phase-commit distributed transaction; sagas are more complex than ACID transactions and only eventually consistent, so any data that must be updated truly atomically has to live within a single service.

In a microservice architecture you cannot obtain a globally consistent view of data across service databases even though each service's database is individually consistent, so data that requires a consistent view must reside in a single service, though in practice this is rarely a problem.

A god class is a bloated class used throughout an application that bundles state and behavior for many different aspects (e.g. Order in e-commerce, Account in banking); because it ties together disparate concerns it is an insurmountable obstacle to splitting the business logic that uses it into services.

Two tempting but bad ways to handle a god class are to package it as a shared library over a central database (which reintroduces tight coupling because a schema change forces lockstep updates) and to hide it behind a single data service (which produces an anemic domain model with little business logic).

Eliminate god classes by applying DDD so that each service is a separate subdomain with its own domain model and its own version of the shared entity (e.g. the Delivery Service's minimal Delivery, the Kitchen Service's Ticket, and the Order Service's Order), then maintain consistency between these per-service objects using sagas.
Because each service has its own domain model, the application must translate between the user experience's own model and each service's model, a translation often handled by the API gateway.

A service API operation exists for one of two reasons: it corresponds to a system operation invoked by external clients (and perhaps other services), or it exists to support collaboration and is invoked only by other services.

A service publishes events primarily to collaborate with other services (for example to implement sagas or to update CQRS views), and it can also use events to notify external clients (for example delivering events to a browser over WebSockets).

When assigning a system operation to a service and the mapping is not obvious, assign it to the service that needs the information the operation provides, or to the service that already holds the information needed to handle it.

A self-contained service handles synchronous requests without synchronously invoking other services, which improves availability; it can be implemented with CQRS (keeping a local replica of another service's data updated by subscribing to that service's events) or with a saga.

Interprocess communication options include synchronous request/response mechanisms (HTTP REST, gRPC) and asynchronous message-based mechanisms (AMQP, STOMP), with message formats ranging from human-readable text (JSON, XML) to efficient binary formats (Avro, Protocol Buffers); the choice of IPC is an important architectural decision that impacts availability and intersects with transaction management.

A recommended default is an architecture of loosely coupled services that communicate with one another using asynchronous messaging, reserving synchronous protocols such as REST mostly for communicating with other (external) applications.

Choose the client-service interaction style before selecting an IPC technology, because the interaction style is technology-independent, keeps focus on requirements, and impacts application availability and the integration-testing strategy.

Client-service interaction styles vary along two dimensions: one-to-one vs one-to-many, and synchronous vs asynchronous; the types include request/response, asynchronous request/response, one-way notification, publish/subscribe, and publish/async-responses.

The synchronous request/response interaction style is largely orthogonal to the IPC technology: a client that blocks waiting for a reply is tightly coupled even when the exchange runs over a message broker, so using messaging does not by itself make services loosely coupled.

A service's API is a contract between the service and its clients; because a service and its clients are not compiled together, deploying an incompatible API change produces runtime failures rather than compile-time errors.

Precisely define every service's API with an interface definition language regardless of the IPC mechanism, and prefer API-first design: write the interface definition, review and iterate it with the client developers, and only then implement the service.

Poorly defined APIs between components (for example between a frontend and backend) cause integration failures even when each side believes it is complete, which is why API-first design matters even on small projects.

Changing a service's API is hard because its clients are other services, other teams, or external applications that cannot be forced to upgrade in lockstep, and rolling upgrades run old and new versions simultaneously, so a controlled versioning strategy is required.

Version APIs with semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH): increment MAJOR for an incompatible change, MINOR for a backward-compatible enhancement, and PATCH for a backward-compatible bug fix; expose the version (e.g. the major version in a REST URL path or in published message payloads).

Strive to make only backward-compatible, additive API changes (adding optional request attributes, adding response attributes, adding new operations) so older clients keep working with newer services, provided both sides follow the Robustness principle: services supply defaults for missing request attributes and clients ignore unknown response attributes.

For unavoidable major, breaking API changes, the service must support the old and new versions simultaneously for a transition period (for example versioning the URL path /v1/ vs /v2/ or negotiating the version via the HTTP MIME type), with adapter logic that translates between versions.
Use a cross-language message format and avoid language-specific serialization such as Java serialization, because even a single-language system today is likely to add other languages later.

Text-based message formats (JSON, XML) are human-readable and self-describing, letting a consumer read the values it wants and ignore the rest so many schema changes stay backward-compatible (and a JSON/XML schema can document and validate messages), at the cost of verbosity and slower parsing.

Binary message formats (Protocol Buffers, Avro) use a typed IDL plus a compiler that generates serialization code, which forces an API-first approach and enables compile-time API checks for statically typed clients; Protocol Buffers' tagged fields make API evolution easier than Avro, which needs the schema to interpret a message.

In the Remote procedure invocation pattern a client invokes a service through a synchronous protocol (such as REST) and assumes a timely response, with a proxy interface that encapsulates the underlying communication protocol.
In REST a resource typically represents a business object or a collection, is referenced by a URL, and is manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to update).

The Richardson REST maturity model has four levels: Level 0 (a single URL, actions via POST), Level 1 (resources), Level 2 (HTTP verbs and status codes, which lets GET requests use web caching), and Level 3 (HATEOAS, where a resource's representation contains links so clients need not hard-wire URLs).

REST's benefits are that it is simple and familiar, testable from a browser or curl, directly supports request/response, is firewall-friendly, and needs no intermediate broker; its drawbacks are that it supports only request/response, reduces availability (both parties must be up with no buffering intermediary), requires clients to know service URLs (needing service discovery), makes fetching multiple resources in one request hard, and makes mapping multiple update operations to HTTP verbs difficult.

gRPC is a binary, Protocol-Buffers-IDL, cross-language RPC framework over HTTP/2 that supports streaming; its benefits are rich update operations, an efficient compact format (especially for large messages), bidirectional streaming, and broad language interoperability, while its drawbacks are harder consumption by JavaScript clients and lack of support by some older firewalls; being synchronous, it still suffers from partial failure.

Whenever a service makes a synchronous request to another service there is an ever-present risk of partial failure (the callee may be down, overloaded, or slow), and a client that blocks waiting for a response can let the failure cascade to its own clients and cause an outage.

Apply the Circuit breaker pattern: an RPI proxy that immediately rejects invocations for a timeout period once consecutive failures exceed a threshold; you must design RPI proxies to handle unresponsive remote services (a naive proxy blocks indefinitely and exhausts resources such as threads) and separately decide how to recover from a failed remote service.

When one service synchronously invokes another, make the RPI proxy robust with three mechanisms: network timeouts (never block indefinitely so resources are never tied up), an upper bound on outstanding requests to a service (fail immediately once reached), and a circuit breaker that trips when the error rate exceeds a threshold and retries after a timeout; use a resilience library such as Netflix Hystrix (JVM) or Polly (.NET).

Beyond using a resilience library, decide on a case-by-case basis how each service recovers from an unresponsive remote service, for example by returning an error to its client or by returning a fallback value such as a default or cached response.

When aggregating data from multiple services (e.g. API composition), handle each dependency's failure by importance: return cached data or an error when essential data is missing, but degrade gracefully by returning cached data or omitting non-critical data so the client still gets a useful response.

In a modern cloud-based microservice application, service instances have dynamically assigned network locations and the instance set changes constantly due to autoscaling, failures, and upgrades, so a client cannot use static configuration and must use a service discovery mechanism.

Service discovery centers on a service registry (a database of the network locations of an application's service instances) that is updated as instances start and stop; when a client invokes a service, the mechanism queries the registry for available instances and routes the request to one of them.

Application-level service discovery combines the Self-registration pattern (a service instance registers its own location, optionally with a health-check URL and heartbeat) and the Client-side discovery pattern (the client queries the registry and load-balances across instances); it works across multiple deployment platforms but requires a discovery library per language/framework and you must operate the registry yourself.

Platform-provided service discovery combines the 3rd-party registration pattern (a registrar in the deployment platform registers instances) and the Server-side discovery pattern (the client calls a DNS name/virtual IP and a router queries the registry and load-balances); it keeps discovery code out of services and clients and works for any language, but only discovers services deployed on that platform. Prefer it whenever possible.
A service instance should expose a health-check URL endpoint that the service registry invokes periodically to verify the instance is healthy and available to handle requests.
In asynchronous messaging, services communicate by exchanging messages (typically through a message broker acting as intermediary) and the client does not block waiting for a reply.

In the messaging model, a sender writes a message to a message channel and a receiver reads from it; a message has a header (name-value metadata including a unique message id and an optional return address) and a body carrying the data in text or binary form.

There are three kinds of messages: a document (data only, the receiver decides how to interpret it), a command (the equivalent of an RPC request, specifying the operation and its parameters), and an event (indicating something notable happened, often a domain event representing a domain object's state change).

There are two kinds of message channels: a point-to-point channel delivers each message to exactly one consumer (used for one-to-one interactions such as commands) and a publish-subscribe channel delivers each message to all attached consumers (used for one-to-many interactions such as events).

Messaging can implement every interaction style: asynchronous request/response by exchanging a request message carrying a reply-channel header and message id and a reply message carrying a correlation id equal to that message id (so the client matches reply to request and knows where the reply goes), one-way notification, publish/subscribe, and publish/async-responses.

Publish domain events to a publish-subscribe channel whose name is derived from the domain class (e.g. the Order Service publishes Order events to an Order channel), and let a service subscribe only to the channels whose events it cares about.

Write an API specification even for an asynchronous, messaging-based API: specify the channel names, the message types exchanged over each channel, and their formats (JSON, XML, or Protobuf); because there is no widely adopted standard like OpenAPI for async APIs, an informal document is required.

A broker-based messaging architecture is usually better than a brokerless one: brokerless messaging (e.g. ZeroMQ) offers lower latency, no broker bottleneck or single point of failure, and less operational complexity, but it requires services to know each other's locations (needing service discovery), reduces availability (both endpoints must be up during the exchange), and makes guarantees such as reliable delivery harder to implement.

When selecting a message broker, evaluate supported languages, supported standards (AMQP/STOMP vs proprietary), message ordering, delivery guarantees, persistence, durability, scalability, latency, and competing-consumer support, recognizing that each broker trades these off (a very low-latency broker may not preserve ordering, guarantee delivery, or persist to disk); message ordering and scalability are usually essential.

Broker-based messaging provides loose coupling (a client just sends to a channel, unaware of service instances and needing no discovery mechanism), message buffering (the broker queues messages so work is accepted even when the consumer is slow or down), support for all interaction styles, and explicit interprocess communication that surfaces partial failure rather than hiding it as RPC does.

The drawbacks of broker-based messaging are that the broker is a potential performance bottleneck and single point of failure (so it must be made highly available) and that it adds operational complexity as another component to install, configure, and operate.

To scale message consumers while preserving ordering, use sharded (partitioned) channels: the sender puts a shard key in the message header, the broker assigns the message to a shard by hashing the key, and the broker assigns each shard to a single instance within a consumer group, so all messages for a given key are processed in order by one consumer.

Because message brokers usually guarantee only at-least-once delivery (exactly-once is too costly), a failure of the client, network, or broker can deliver a message more than once (e.g. a consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging), so the application must be designed to handle duplicate messages.

Handle duplicate messages in one of two ways: write idempotent message handlers that can be safely re-executed with the same input (e.g. cancelling an already-cancelled order), or, when the logic is not idempotent or the broker does not preserve redelivery ordering, track processed message ids and discard duplicates.

Implement duplicate detection by recording each processed message id within the same local transaction that updates the business entities (for example inserting the id into a PROCESSED_MESSAGES table so a duplicate insert fails), storing ids in a dedicated table or, for a NoSQL store with a limited transaction model, in an application table.

A service must update its database and publish its messages atomically, because doing them separately risks the database committing and the service crashing before the message is sent, leaving the system inconsistent; distributed transactions spanning the database and broker are a poor choice and many brokers (e.g. Kafka) do not support them.

Apply the Transactional outbox pattern to publish messages reliably: within the local ACID transaction that updates business objects, insert each outgoing message into an OUTBOX table (guaranteeing atomicity), and have a separate Message Relay read the OUTBOX and publish the messages to the broker (a NoSQL variant appends the message to the entity record).

The Polling publisher pattern moves messages from the outbox by having the Message Relay periodically query the OUTBOX for unpublished messages, publish them, and delete them; it is simple and works at low scale but frequent polling is expensive and may not work efficiently on a NoSQL database.

The Transaction log tailing pattern moves messages by having a miner read the database's transaction (commit) log and publish each relevant change (such as an OUTBOX insert) as a message; it is more performant and scalable than polling but requires more implementation effort (e.g. via Debezium or DynamoDB streams).

Avoid using a message broker's low-level client library directly, because it couples the business logic to broker APIs, requires boilerplate, and lacks higher-level interaction styles; instead use a higher-level messaging library or framework that hides the low-level details and directly supports styles such as asynchronous request/response and domain-event publishing.

Synchronous inter-service communication during request handling reduces availability: the availability of a system operation is the mathematical product of the availabilities of all services it synchronously invokes, so each additional synchronously invoked service further lowers overall availability (e.g. three services at 99.5% yield 98.5%).

Reduced availability from synchronous calls is not specific to REST; it occurs whenever a service can respond only after receiving a response from another service, even over request/response messaging, so to maximize availability you must minimize synchronous communication.

One way to eliminate synchronous interaction is to define services that expose only asynchronous APIs; because this is not always possible (public APIs are commonly RESTful), a service may need a synchronous external API while still avoiding synchronous calls to other services internally.

A service can handle a synchronous external request without making synchronous calls by using asynchronous interaction styles internally: it exchanges messages with other services and eventually replies to the client, so no participant blocks and the broker's buffering makes the architecture resilient.

To reduce synchronous calls, a service can replicate the data it needs locally and keep the replica up to date by subscribing to change events from the owning services, but replication is inefficient for large data volumes and does not solve how a service updates data owned by other services.

A service can eliminate synchronous communication during request handling by finishing processing after returning a response: validate using only local data, update its database (including inserting OUTBOX messages), return a response, and then interact with other services asynchronously (often via a saga); the trade-off is a more complex client that must poll or receive a notification because the response is returned before processing completes.

ACID transactions simplify development by giving each transaction the illusion of exclusive data access; a transaction within a single service can still be ACID, but an operation that updates data owned by multiple services needs a cross-service transaction mechanism.

Even monolithic applications rarely use textbook ACID transactions (many lower the isolation level for performance and many important business processes such as inter-bank transfers are eventually consistent), so eventual consistency should not be treated as unacceptable.

Distributed transactions (the X/Open XA two-phase-commit model) are not a viable choice for modern applications: many modern technologies (NoSQL databases like MongoDB and Cassandra, brokers like RabbitMQ and Kafka) do not support them, and being synchronous IPC they reduce availability (which is the product of all participants' availability); given the CAP theorem, architects today usually prefer availability over strong consistency.

Use the Saga pattern for every system command that must update data in multiple services: a saga is a sequence of local ACID transactions, each updating a single service's database, coordinated by asynchronous messaging so that completing one local transaction triggers the next.

Coordinating a saga with asynchronous messaging guarantees the saga eventually completes even if a participant is temporarily unavailable, because the message broker buffers the triggering message until it can be delivered.

Sagas are ACD rather than ACID (they lack the isolation property), and because each local transaction commits its changes immediately, a saga cannot be automatically rolled back and must be undone with explicit compensating transactions.

When step n+1 of a saga fails, undo the committed effects of the previous n steps by executing their compensating transactions in reverse order (C_n through C_1); the saga's coordination logic is responsible for sequencing both the forward and the compensating transactions.
Not every saga step requires a compensating transaction: read-only steps and steps that are always followed by steps that succeed do not need one.

Classify saga steps into compensatable transactions (they are followed by steps that can fail, so they need compensating transactions), a single pivot transaction (the go/no-go point, followed only by steps that never fail), and retriable transactions (which always succeed and follow the pivot).

A saga's coordination logic can be structured in two ways: choreography, which distributes decision-making and sequencing among the participants that communicate by exchanging events with no central coordinator, or orchestration, which centralizes the logic in a saga orchestrator that sends command messages telling participants what to do.
In a choreography-based saga, each participant updates its own database and then publishes an event that triggers the next participant, which has subscribed to the relevant events.

In a choreography-based saga, each participant must update its database and publish its triggering event atomically using transactional messaging, otherwise a crash between the two leaves the saga in an inconsistent state.

In a choreography-based saga, a participant must be able to map each event it receives back to its own data, achieved by publishing events that carry a correlation id (such as an orderId passed from one participant to the next).

Choreography-based sagas are simple and loosely coupled (participants just publish and subscribe to events), but they are harder to understand because no single place defines the saga, they tend to create cyclic dependencies between services (a design smell), and they risk tight coupling because a participant must subscribe to every event that affects it.

In an orchestration-based saga, an orchestrator class whose sole responsibility is coordination uses command/async-reply interaction: it sends a command to a participant, receives a reply, and then determines the next step.

Model a saga orchestrator as a state machine (states plus event-triggered transitions whose actions invoke saga participants), because it captures all of the saga's scenarios and makes the saga easier to design, implement, and test.

Orchestration-based sagas avoid cyclic dependencies (participants do not invoke the orchestrator), reduce coupling (participants expose an API and need not know each other's events), and localize coordination logic so domain objects stay simple; their one drawback is the risk of centralizing too much business logic in a smart orchestrator, which is avoided by keeping the orchestrator responsible only for sequencing.
Use orchestration for all but the simplest sagas; choreography is acceptable for simple sagas but its drawbacks make orchestration preferable as sagas grow complex.

Sagas lack the isolation property of ACID transactions because each local transaction's updates become visible to other sagas as soon as it commits, so a saga is ACD (atomicity, consistency, durability) and concurrent sagas can read or overwrite one another's in-flight data.

The lack of isolation between sagas can cause three anomalies: lost updates (one saga overwrites another's change without reading it), dirty reads (a saga reads another saga's uncommitted in-flight updates), and fuzzy/nonrepeatable reads (two steps of a saga read the same data and differ because another saga updated it in between); lost updates and dirty reads are the most common and most challenging.

It is the developer's responsibility to write sagas that either prevent isolation anomalies or minimize their business impact by applying countermeasures, some of which implement isolation at the application level and others of which reduce the business risk.

The documented countermeasures for the saga lack of isolation are the semantic lock (an application-level lock), commutative updates (operations executable in any order), pessimistic view (reordering saga steps to minimize risk), reread value (verifying data is unchanged before overwriting to prevent lost updates), version file (recording updates so they can be reordered), and by value (selecting the concurrency mechanism per request based on business risk).

The semantic lock countermeasure has a compensatable transaction set a flag (such as an *_PENDING state) on records it creates or updates to signal that the record is uncommitted and may change; a retriable transaction clears the flag on success and a compensating transaction clears it on rollback, and you must decide per case how a saga handles a locked record (fail-and-tell-the-client-to-retry, which is simple but pushes retry logic to the client, or block until the lock is released, which recreates ACID-like isolation but requires lock management and deadlock detection).

The commutative updates countermeasure designs update operations to be commutative (executable in any order, such as credit and debit) so that a compensating transaction can simply apply the inverse, which eliminates lost updates.
The pessimistic view countermeasure reorders the steps of a saga to minimize the business risk arising from a dirty read.
When migrating a monolith into sagas it is significantly simpler if the monolith only ever needs to execute retriable transactions, which never require rollback.

The reread value countermeasure (a form of the Optimistic Offline Lock pattern) prevents lost updates by rereading a record before updating it, verifying it is unchanged, and only then updating; if the record has changed the saga aborts and possibly restarts.

The version file countermeasure records the operations performed on a record so they can be reordered, turning noncommutative operations into commutative ones (for example a service that receives a cancel-authorization before the corresponding authorize records the cancel and then skips the later authorize).

The by value countermeasure selects the concurrency mechanism per request based on business risk: execute low-risk requests as sagas (with countermeasures) but high-risk requests, such as those involving large amounts of money, as distributed transactions, dynamically trading off business risk against availability and scalability.

A single service can be both a saga orchestrator and a saga participant; when a service participates in its own saga it uses a command-handler adapter that handles command messages by invoking its own domain service, treating itself as just another participant for consistency.

A service method that starts a saga should run in one transaction that creates and persists the entity, publishes its domain events, and creates and persists the saga orchestrator, so the entity and its saga are created atomically.

Define a saga participant's messaging API with a statically typed proxy class (specifying the command channel, command types, and reply types): although not strictly necessary, it reduces the chance of sending the wrong message to a service and provides a well-defined, testable interface that enables narrowly scoped tests verifying one service correctly invokes another.

Implement a saga as a persisted state machine driven by a saga framework that persists the saga instance state, sends the command messages it generates, subscribes to reply messages, executes the next step on each reply, and executes compensating transactions in reverse order when a participant fails.
Define each saga step declaratively together with its onReply handler and its compensating transaction, so the forward transaction and the compensation for a step are specified in one place.

Designing business logic in a microservice architecture has two key challenges: a typical domain model is a tangled web of interconnected classes, so object references that would span service boundaries must be eliminated, and the business logic must work within the transaction model (ACID within a service, sagas across services).

The DDD Aggregate pattern structures a service's business logic as a collection of aggregates, which fit microservices because inter-aggregate references are primary-key values (so no object reference spans a service boundary) and a transaction creates or updates a single aggregate (so an ACID transaction stays within one service).

The Transaction Script pattern organizes business logic as procedural transaction scripts (one per request) in service classes, with behavior separated from largely behavior-free data classes accessed via DAOs; it works well for simple business logic but is a poor way to implement complex business logic.

The Domain Model pattern organizes business logic as an object model of small classes that map to domain concepts and mostly have both state and behavior, keeping service methods simple by delegating to persistent domain objects that hold the bulk of the logic.

Unless an application's business logic is very simple, prefer the object-oriented Domain Model pattern over procedural transaction scripts, because it is easier to understand and maintain (small single-responsibility classes mirroring the domain), easier to test (each class independently), and easier to extend (via patterns such as Strategy and Template Method).

DDD's widely adopted tactical building blocks are the Entity (an object with a persistent identity, so two entities with equal attributes are still distinct), the Value Object (a collection of values, so two with equal attributes are interchangeable, e.g. Money), the Factory (creation logic too complex for a constructor), the Repository (encapsulates database access to persistent entities), and the Service (business logic that belongs in neither an entity nor a value object).
A traditional domain model modeled as a web of interconnected classes leaves the boundaries of each business object implicit, which causes problems especially in a microservice architecture.

Fuzzy business-object boundaries cause invariant violations: without an explicit boundary and a single enforcement point, two concurrent updates to different parts of the same business object can each individually satisfy an invariant (e.g. an order minimum) yet together violate it.

An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects within a boundary that is treated as a unit, consisting of a root entity plus possibly other entities and value objects; load, update, and delete operations act on the whole aggregate, which clarifies operation scope and avoids lazy-loading complications.

Aggregates are consistency boundaries: update operations must be invoked on the aggregate root, which enforces the aggregate's invariants, and concurrency is handled by locking the root (via a version number or a database lock) rather than updating parts of the aggregate directly.
A key part of designing a domain model is identifying the aggregates, their boundaries, and their roots; the details of an aggregate's internal structure are secondary.

Aggregate rule 1 (reference only the aggregate root): the root entity is the only part of an aggregate that classes outside it may reference, and a client updates the aggregate only by invoking a method on the root, which ensures the aggregate can enforce its invariants.

Aggregate rule 2 (inter-aggregate references use primary keys): aggregates reference each other by identity (e.g. a stored id) rather than object references, which keeps aggregates loosely coupled with well-defined boundaries, avoids accidentally updating another aggregate, prevents object references spanning services, and simplifies persistence and sharding; this reverses the traditional view that foreign keys in a domain model are a design smell.

Aggregate rule 3 (one transaction creates or updates one aggregate) keeps a transaction contained within a single service and matches the limited transaction model of most NoSQL databases; operations that must change multiple aggregates use a saga whose each step touches exactly one aggregate, except that within one service on a rich-transaction RDBMS you may update multiple aggregates in a single transaction.
exception: on an RDBMS with a rich transaction model, multiple aggregates within a single service may be updated in one transaction instead of via a saga

statement: Choose aggregate granularity deliberately: prefer small, fine-grained aggregates because updates to each aggregate are serialized (so finer aggregates raise concurrency and scalability and reduce conflicting-update collisions), but a larger aggregate may be required to make a particular update atomic; because a larger aggregate reduces scalability and obstructs decomposition, keep aggregates as fine-grained as possible.

In a typical service the bulk of the business logic resides in aggregates, with the remainder in domain services (the entry points invoked by inbound adapters) and sagas (which orchestrate local transactions for cross-service consistency); a service uses a repository, implemented by an outbound adapter, to load and save aggregates.
The Domain event pattern has an aggregate publish a domain event when it is created or undergoes a significant state change, with the event represented by a class in the domain model.

Publish domain events because many parties care about an aggregate's state changes: coordinating choreography-based sagas, updating CQRS replicas, triggering other applications via webhook or broker, updating other components of the same application (e.g. a search index or a WebSocket push), sending user notifications, monitoring, and analytics.

A domain event class is named with a past-participle verb and has properties (primitive values or value objects) that convey what happened, and it typically carries metadata such as an event id, a timestamp, and often the identity of the user who made the change for auditing, either on the event or in an enclosing envelope.

Apply event enrichment by including in an event the data its consumers need so they need not call back to the publishing service, accepting the trade-off that enriched event classes are less stable and must change as consumer requirements change, which can reduce maintainability.

Identify domain events from requirements phrased as 'when X happens do Y' (a notification requirement implies a domain event) or through event storming, an event-centric workshop that brainstorms events onto a timeline, identifies each event's trigger (a user command, an external system, another event, or the passing of time), and then identifies the aggregate that consumes each command and emits the event.

Do not have an aggregate call the messaging API directly, because aggregates cannot use dependency injection and doing so would intertwine infrastructure with business logic; instead have the aggregate generate events on state change and return them (or accumulate them in a field), and have the service, which can inject the publisher, publish them.

Publish domain events reliably using transactional messaging: insert the events into an OUTBOX table within the same ACID transaction that updates the aggregate, and publish them to the broker after the transaction commits.

Publish domain events through a type-safe, per-aggregate publisher restricted to that aggregate's event marker interface rather than calling a generic publisher directly, so a service can only publish events valid for its aggregate.

Consume domain events with a higher-level dispatcher that maps aggregate type and event type to handler methods rather than the broker's raw client API; a common use is keeping a service's local replica of another service's data up to date.

Each service's aggregate should model only its own bounded-context view of a shared business object (for example a kitchen's Ticket omits consumer identity, delivery, and payment and focuses on preparing the order) and can reuse an id supplied by the owning service rather than generating its own.

Model an aggregate's lifecycle as an explicit state machine: each state-changing method validates the current state, performs the transition (recording relevant timestamps), and returns a domain event, throwing an exception on a disallowed transition (for example an order cannot be cancelled once the restaurant has begun preparing it).
Use an optimistic-locking version field on an aggregate root to detect concurrent modification of the aggregate.

An operation that requires a saga should first transition its aggregate to a *_PENDING state (a semantic-lock countermeasure that isolates concurrent sagas), then transition to the success state after the saga verifies the operation, reverting to the previous state if verification fails.

Structure an aggregate's methods in groups per saga, with one method invoked at the saga's start (moving the aggregate to a pending state) and other methods invoked at the saga's end to confirm or reject the outcome.

A create or update service method whose operation spans services should create and persist the aggregate, publish its domain events, and then create a saga, rather than updating the aggregate directly, because the aggregate must be kept transactionally consistent with data owned by other services.

Business logic in a microservice application is largely similar to a monolith's (services, persistent entities, repositories) but differs in that the domain model is a set of DDD aggregates, inter-aggregate references are by primary key, a transaction creates or updates a single aggregate, aggregates publish domain events on state change, and services often use sagas for cross-service consistency.

A service may only participate in sagas (like a kitchen service) or heavily initiate them (like an order service); a service must initiate sagas when its data has to be kept transactionally consistent with data owned by other services.

With traditional persistence, the event-publishing logic is bolted onto the business logic, so the business logic still appears to work if a developer forgets to publish an event, which is a source of bugs.
The Event sourcing pattern persists an aggregate as a sequence of domain events, each representing a state change, and recreates the aggregate's current state by replaying those events.

Event sourcing preserves the complete history of each aggregate (valuable for auditing and regulatory purposes) and reliably publishes a domain event whenever an aggregate is created or updated, which eliminates the class of bug where a developer forgets to publish an event.
Event sourcing has drawbacks: a learning curve because it is a different way of writing business logic, and difficulty querying the event store, which forces the use of the CQRS pattern for queries.

Traditional persistence has four limitations: the object-relational impedance mismatch between a tabular schema and an object graph, storing only the current state (so aggregate history is lost and must be hand-built), tedious and error-prone audit logging that can diverge from the business logic, and event publishing that is bolted on and must be manually kept in sync with the business logic.

Event sourcing persists each aggregate as a sequence of events in an event store, and loads an aggregate by fetching its events, instantiating it with its default constructor, and replaying the events by calling apply() (a fold/reduce over the events).

With event sourcing, emitting events is not optional: every state change of an aggregate, including its creation, must emit a domain event, and it is primarily the aggregate (not the consumers) that determines the events and their structure.

Each event must contain the data needed to perform the state transition it represents, so that applying event E to state S yields state S'; consequently an event-sourced OrderCreated event must carry all initialization data rather than being a minimal id-only event.

Event sourcing splits each command method into a process() method that validates a command and returns events without changing state (throwing if the command cannot be performed) and one or more apply() methods that each take a single event type and update state and cannot fail, because the event represents a change that has already happened.

Create an event-sourced aggregate by instantiating it with its default constructor, calling process() to generate events, applying those events, and saving them; update it by loading and replaying its events, calling process() for new events, applying them, and saving the new events.

Handle concurrent updates to an event-sourced aggregate with optimistic locking: read a version along with the aggregate's events and, on insert, have the event store verify the version is unchanged (a simple scheme uses the number of events as the version).

Event sourcing doubles as a reliable event-publishing mechanism because saving an event is atomic; persisted events are delivered to consumers by polling or transaction log tailing, differing from the transactional outbox only in that events are stored permanently in an EVENTS table rather than temporarily in an OUTBOX.

Naive polling for new events by event id greater than the last seen id can skip events because transactions can commit out of event-id order (a later id commits and is read first, then the earlier id becomes visible and is missed); prevent this by adding a PUBLISHED flag column, polling for unpublished events, and marking them published after sending.
Transaction log tailing is a more sophisticated event-publishing approach than polling that guarantees events are published and is more performant and scalable.

For long-lived aggregates that accumulate many events, loading and folding all events becomes inefficient, so periodically persist a snapshot of the aggregate's state and load only the snapshot plus the events that occurred after it.

Restore an event-sourced aggregate from a snapshot by recreating the instance from the snapshot and then applying only the events that occurred after it; snapshot a simple aggregate via JSON serialization and a complex one via the Memento pattern.

For idempotent message processing with an RDBMS-based event store, insert the message id into a PROCESSED_MESSAGES table within the same transaction that inserts the events, and discard any message whose id is already recorded.

For idempotent message processing with a NoSQL-based event store (which has a limited transaction model), store the processed message's id in the events it generates and detect a duplicate by checking whether any of the aggregate's events already contains that id.

When processing a message that generates no events, there is no record it was handled, so its redelivery can be reprocessed and cause incorrect behavior; avoid this by always emitting an event, saving a pseudo-event solely to record the message id when the aggregate would otherwise emit none (and having consumers ignore pseudo-events).

An event-sourcing application's schema evolves at three levels (aggregate types, the event types an aggregate emits, and event field structure); additive changes such as a new aggregate type, a new event type, or a new field are backward-compatible, while removing, renaming, or retyping is not.

Handle non-backward-compatible event changes with an upcaster that transforms each event from an old version to the current version when it is loaded from the event store, so aggregate code only ever deals with the current event schema and version-handling stays out of the aggregate.

Event sourcing's benefits are reliably publishing domain events (a foundation for event-driven microservices and an accurate audit log that can record the acting user), preserving each aggregate's full history (enabling temporal queries by folding events up to a point in time), mostly avoiding the object-relational impedance mismatch, and acting as a time machine that lets developers satisfy unanticipated requirements from past data.

Event sourcing's drawbacks are an unfamiliar programming model with a learning curve (existing business logic must be rewritten), the complexity of a messaging application (at-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers, e.g. tracking the highest-seen event id), tricky event evolution, tricky data deletion, and challenging queries against the event store.

Delete data in an event-sourced system with a soft delete (set a deleted flag and emit a Deleted event), and satisfy GDPR right-to-erasure by encrypting each user's personal-data events with a per-user key that is deleted to render those events unreadable, using pseudonymization (mapping a UUID token to the personal data) when personal data is used as an aggregate id.

Querying an event store directly is challenging because state (such as a credit limit) is not a queryable column but must be folded from events, and NoSQL event stores typically support only primary-key lookup, so such queries must be implemented with the CQRS pattern.

An event store is a hybrid of a database (an API to insert and retrieve an aggregate's events by primary key) and a message broker (an API to subscribe to events); you can build your own or use a special-purpose store such as Event Store, Lagom, Axon, or Eventuate.

Store an event store's events with a topic (a partitioned message channel) per aggregate type and use the aggregate id as the partition key, so that events from a given aggregate stay ordered while consumers scale horizontally.

Propagate events from the event database to the message broker with an event relay that uses transaction log tailing where possible (e.g. reading the MySQL binlog) and polling otherwise, and that periodically checkpoints its log position so it can restart correctly.

Event sourcing makes choreography-based sagas straightforward because it supplies exactly what they need: messaging-based IPC, automatic message de-duplication, and atomic updating of state with message sending, so an aggregate emits an event on update and another aggregate's idempotent event handler consumes it and updates its own aggregate.

Using events for saga choreography gives events a dual purpose (representing state changes and signaling the saga), which forces an aggregate to emit an event even when there is no state change (e.g. to report a business-rule violation) and leaves no aggregate to emit an error when a participant cannot be created, so complex sagas are better implemented with orchestration.

Integrating orchestration-based sagas with event sourcing depends on the event store: an RDBMS-based event store can update the store and the saga framework within one ACID transaction, but a NoSQL-based event store's limited transaction model cannot, requiring a different event-driven approach.

Create a saga orchestrator reliably from an event-sourced service by using an event handler that responds to the aggregate's creation event rather than creating the saga in the same transaction; this event-driven creation works with both NoSQL and RDBMS event stores and promotes loose coupling by not having services explicitly instantiate sagas.

An event handler that creates a saga must tolerate duplicate events (at-least-once delivery) so that exactly one saga instance is created, achieved by deriving the saga id from a unique event attribute: the emitting aggregate's id for creation-triggered sagas, or the unique event id when multiple sagas per aggregate are possible.
An event-sourcing saga participant achieves idempotent command handling by recording the command message's id in the events it generates and checking for that id before updating the aggregate.

An event-sourcing saga participant sends its reply atomically by saving a SagaReplyRequested pseudo-event alongside the aggregate's real events and having an event handler for that pseudo-event construct and send the reply, which avoids the problems of the orchestrator subscribing to aggregate events (no reply when a command causes no state change, and special-casing event-sourced participants).

Persist a saga orchestrator with event sourcing via SagaOrchestratorCreated and SagaOrchestratorUpdated events that carry the serialized orchestrator state, which lets an application be built entirely on an event store.

An event-sourcing saga orchestrator sends commands reliably with a two-step pseudo-event process (emit a SagaCommandEvent per command, and an event handler sends the actual command), guaranteeing at-least-once delivery, and deduplicates by using the unique SagaCommandEvent id as the command message id and by storing each reply's id in the events it emits to process replies exactly once.

Queries are a distinct distributed-data challenge in a microservice architecture because a query often needs data scattered across multiple services' databases, and a traditional distributed query cannot be used since it would violate service encapsulation.
