Two patterns implement queries in a microservice architecture: the API composition pattern (the simplest, in which a client of the data-owning services invokes them and combines the results, and which should be used whenever possible) and the CQRS pattern (more powerful but more complex, maintaining one or more view databases whose sole purpose is to support queries).
The API composition pattern implements a multi-service query with an API composer that invokes the provider services owning the data and combines their results.

Whether API composition can implement a given query depends on how the data is partitioned and the capabilities of the providers' APIs and databases; it may require an inefficient in-memory join of large datasets, and some queries cannot be implemented with it at all.

There are three options for who plays the API composer: a client (efficient only over a fast/LAN network, not for clients outside the firewall), an API gateway (when the query is part of the external API, so one call gathers data from many services), or a standalone service (for a query used by multiple services or whose aggregation logic is too complex for the gateway).

An API composer should invoke provider services in parallel wherever the calls have no dependencies to minimize response time (invoking sequentially only when one result feeds another) and should use a reactive design such as CompletableFuture or RxJava to remain maintainable and performant.

The API composition pattern has three drawbacks: increased overhead from multiple service requests and database queries, reduced availability (which declines with the number of services, e.g. one composer plus four providers each at 99.5% yields 97.5%), and lack of transactional consistency (queries across multiple databases can return inconsistent data the composer may not even detect).

Improve an API composer's availability by returning previously cached (possibly stale) data when a provider is unavailable, or by returning incomplete data that omits an unavailable non-critical provider so the UI can still show useful information.
The CQRS pattern implements a query that needs data from several services by using events to maintain one or more read-only view databases that replicate the data and exist solely to support queries.

Use CQRS when any of three problems arises: API composition would require expensive in-memory joins, the owning service stores its data in a form or database that does not efficiently support the query, or separation of concerns means the service that owns the data should not implement the query.

Do not build a query-execution engine inside an API composer (joining, filtering, and sorting large datasets in memory because providers lack the needed attributes), because it duplicates an RDBMS's query engine, is inefficient, and diverts developers from business functionality; use CQRS instead.

A query local to a single service can still be hard when the owning service's database does not efficiently support it (for example a geospatial search needs a geospatially capable store and index), in which case maintain a query-optimized replica kept up to date via CQRS.

The service that owns data should not necessarily implement a high-volume, critical query over that data, because doing so overloads the owning team with unrelated responsibility and risks a routine change breaking a critical path; instead have it provide the data to a separate query service.

CQRS splits the persistent model and its modules into a command side that handles create/update/delete and publishes domain events (and may still serve simple primary-key queries) and a query side that serves queries only and keeps its data model synchronized by subscribing to the command side's events.

CQRS can define query-only services whose API has only query operations and which maintain a database by subscribing to events from one or more services, which is a good way to implement a view that spans multiple services (belonging to none) or a view that replicates a single service's data but is separated from it to keep concerns apart.

CQRS's benefits are that it efficiently implements multi-service queries with a pre-joined view (avoiding in-memory joins), efficiently implements diverse queries by letting each view use a database specialized for it, enables querying in an event-sourced application (which otherwise supports only primary-key lookup, so event-sourced applications invariably use CQRS), and improves separation of concerns by giving the command and query sides separate modules and schemas and letting the querying service differ from the owning one.

CQRS's drawbacks are a more complex architecture (extra query-side services and datastores, possibly of multiple types) and replication lag between the command and query sides (a client that updates and then immediately queries may see the old version), so use API composition whenever possible and CQRS only when necessary.

Handle CQRS replication lag by giving the client version information: a command returns a token (the published event id) that the client passes to the query, which returns an error until the view has applied that event so the client can poll until up to date; alternatively a UI can update its local model from the command's result without issuing a query.

A CQRS view module consists of a view database plus three submodules: event handlers that subscribe to events and update the database, a query API module, and a data access module that implements the database-access logic used by the other two.

Choose a CQRS view's datastore by the characteristics of its queries (and of its event-handler updates): a NoSQL database is often a good fit because a view needs only simple transactions and a fixed query set while benefiting from a rich data model and performance, though a SQL database may be preferable for familiarity or reporting; match the store type to the query kind (document store for primary-key/JSON lookup, text search engine for text, graph database for graph queries, RDBMS for BI).

A CQRS view's data model must efficiently support the event handlers' update operations, not just its queries: most updates are by primary key, but some require foreign-key-based updates (e.g. updating an order record from an event that carries only a deliveryId), which need an index on relational or document databases or an application-maintained foreign-key-to-primary-key mapping on stores that only support primary-key updates.

A CQRS view that subscribes to a single aggregate type has no concurrency problem because an instance's events are processed sequentially, but a view that joins multiple aggregate types can have concurrent updates to the same record, so its DAO must not let one update overwrite another, using pessimistic or optimistic locking or blind updates that do not read first.

CQRS event handlers must be idempotent so that a duplicate event yields the correct outcome: a naturally idempotent handler may leave the view temporarily stale, while a non-idempotent handler (e.g. incrementing a balance) must detect and discard duplicates by recording processed event ids in the view store atomically with the view update.

Deduplicating CQRS events need not record every event id: with monotonically increasing ids, store the max event id per aggregate instance, and only records that join events from multiple aggregates need a map from [aggregate type, aggregate id] to max event id.

Build or rebuild a CQRS view by processing events, but do not rely on the message broker alone because brokers do not retain events indefinitely; also read older archived events (e.g. from object storage such as S3) using a scalable big-data technology such as Apache Spark.

Build CQRS views incrementally with a two-step algorithm (periodically snapshot each aggregate from its prior snapshot plus subsequent events, then build the view from the snapshots plus later events), because processing all events from scratch grows too slow and expensive over time.

In a NoSQL CQRS view the queries dictate the schema, so design tables and indexes around the required access patterns (for example a composite partition-plus-sort key and a secondary index carrying non-key attributes to support a sorted, filtered, multi-item query).

Update a view record by modifying individual attributes without first reading the whole record (e.g. DynamoDB's UpdateItem rather than PutItem), which both avoids lost updates when concurrent event handlers touch different attributes and is more efficient than a read-modify-write.

Make view updates idempotent with a conditional update: track the highest processed event id per aggregate instance in the record and apply the update only when the incoming event id is greater (or the tracking attribute is absent), so duplicate events are ignored.
Paginate query results with an opaque continuation token that the client passes back to fetch the next page, rather than position-based offsets.

Designing an application's external API is hard because clients are diverse: different clients need different data (a desktop UI shows more than a mobile app) and reach the services over different networks (a fast LAN inside the firewall versus the slower internet or mobile network outside), so a single one-size-fits-all API often does not make sense.

Having external clients invoke services directly is rarely used in a microservice architecture because fine-grained service APIs force clients into many requests (inefficient, poor UX), clients knowing each service and its API breaks encapsulation and makes the architecture hard to change, and services may use IPC mechanisms that are inconvenient or impractical for clients (especially outside the firewall).

A chatty client-to-services API hurts mobile user experience because high-latency mobile and internet networks (roughly 100x LAN latency) make any sequential requests slow, it forces complex API-composition code onto client developers, and each network request drains the device battery.

Baking knowledge of the services into a mobile application makes API evolution hard, because a new mobile version takes days to roll out (app-store approval, and users may never upgrade) unlike a server-side application, so exposing service APIs directly to mobile clients obstructs changing those APIs.

External clients outside the firewall typically speak HTTP and WebSockets, but backend services may use client-unfriendly or non-firewall-friendly protocols such as gRPC or AMQP, which makes direct client access to services impractical.

A server-side web application inside the firewall can access backend services directly because LAN bandwidth and latency are adequate, it can use non-web protocols, and it is updated in lockstep with the backend, whereas browser JavaScript and third-party applications reach services over the internet and suffer the same latency and inefficient-composition problems as mobile clients.

An API used by third-party developers must be kept stable and carefully version-managed (often maintaining old versions indefinitely) because you can rarely force third parties to upgrade, so expose a separate public API built by a separate team (an API gateway) rather than the backend services directly.

The API gateway pattern is a single service that is the entry point into the application from outside the firewall, responsible for request routing, API composition, and protocol translation, and (like a Facade) encapsulates the internal architecture and presents clients an API.

An API gateway routes requests by consulting a routing map (e.g. HTTP method and path to a service URL) like a reverse proxy, and must route by HTTP method when the application uses separate CQRS command and query services.

Provide each client type with its own client-specific API rather than a single one-size-fits-all API, because clients have different needs (mobile needs a subset, a third party needs full details); letting clients select fields is adequate only for a broad public API.

An API gateway may implement edge functions (authentication, authorization, rate limiting, caching, metrics collection, request logging); authenticate at the edge before requests reach the services for better security, and implementing edge functions in the gateway itself (rather than a separate upstream edge service) removes a network hop and reduces complexity at the cost of centralization.

Do not make a single API-gateway team own all API modules (a centralized bottleneck like an SOA ESB team that is counter to autonomous teams); instead have each client team own its API module while an API-gateway team owns the common layer and operations, which requires a fully automated deployment pipeline.

The Backends for Frontends (BFF) pattern implements a separate API gateway per client type, each owned and operated by that client team, which gives clear ownership, fault isolation (one misbehaving API cannot hurt others), better observability, independent scalability, and faster startup; ideally all BFFs share one technology stack with common edge functions in a shared library.

An API gateway's benefits are that it encapsulates the internal structure (clients talk to the gateway, not services), gives each client a client-specific API that reduces round-trips, and simplifies client code; its drawbacks are that it is another highly available component to build, deploy, and manage and risks becoming a development bottleneck, so the process for updating it must be lightweight and automated.

Choosing synchronous versus asynchronous I/O is a key API-gateway design decision: thread-per-connection synchronous I/O is simple but limited by heavyweight OS threads, while non-blocking event-loop I/O is far more scalable but its callback model is harder to write and debug (handlers must return quickly), and non-blocking helps I/O-intensive routing but not CPU-intensive work.

Write API-composition code so that independent service calls run concurrently rather than sequentially (sequential response time is the sum of the calls), and use declarative reactive abstractions such as CompletableFuture, Project Reactor Mono, or RxJava rather than raw callbacks to avoid callback hell and keep mixed parallel/sequential composition maintainable.

Make an API gateway reliable by running multiple instances behind a load balancer and by using the Circuit breaker pattern when it invokes services, because an outstanding request to a failed or slow service can consume a precious resource such as a thread and leave the gateway unable to serve other requests.
An API gateway must be a good citizen in the architecture by implementing the same service-discovery and observability patterns chosen for that architecture.

There are two ways to implement an API gateway: use an off-the-shelf product or service (little development but least flexible, and often lacking API composition) or build your own on an API-gateway or web framework (most flexible but requiring development effort).

Off-the-shelf API gateways (e.g. AWS API Gateway, AWS Application Load Balancer, Kong, Traefik) provide routing and edge functions with little development but are the least flexible and typically do not support API composition, so if you need composition you must build your own gateway or do the composition in the backend services.

Building your own API gateway requires solving two design problems, a mechanism for defining routing rules that minimizes complex coding and correct HTTP proxying including header handling, so start from a purpose-built gateway framework rather than a bare web framework to reduce the code.

A gateway that supports only path-based routing (such as Netflix Zuul) cannot route by HTTP method (e.g. GET /orders versus POST /orders to different services), so it cannot support a CQRS architecture with separate command and query services; prefer a gateway that routes on method, headers, and path.

Structure a custom API gateway into a main module, one or more API packages (each implementing a client's endpoints), and a proxy package of proxy classes that invoke the services, and externalize the backend service URLs via configuration such as properties files or environment variables.

Write a gateway's API-composition handlers in a reactive style (for example Project Reactor Mono or Java CompletableFuture) that invokes the services in parallel and combines the results without callback hell, where a Mono represents the outcome of an asynchronous operation (a value or an exception) with a rich API for transforming and combining values.

Improve a gateway's availability by treating non-essential provider results as optional in the composition, for example mapping a failed provider call to an empty value so that one unavailable service does not fail the whole response.

Implementing a REST gateway that serves diverse clients well is time-consuming (per-client field/expand parameters or separate BFF endpoint versions), so consider a graph-based API framework such as GraphQL or Netflix Falcor whose server exposes a graph schema of typed nodes with fields and relationships, letting a client fetch exactly the data it needs in a single round-trip.

A graph-based API gives clients control over what data is returned, so one flexible API can support diverse clients, and it reduces development effort because the query-execution framework handles the composition and projection.

A GraphQL-based API gateway centers on a schema (a typed data model plus the queries and mutations clients may run), resolver functions that map schema elements to the backend services, and proxy classes that invoke those services.

A GraphQL server executes a query by recursively invoking resolver functions attached to schema fields (first the top-level query resolver, then the resolvers for the fields of each result object), so the engine implements the API composition pattern by having resolvers call one or more backend services.

Optimize GraphQL resolvers with server-side batching (coalescing N per-object service calls into one batch call) and caching (reusing a prior fetch of the same object) to avoid the N+1 round-trip problem, using per-request loader instances so different users' data cannot be mixed.

Manual testing is broken because it is inefficient (humans are slow and cannot work continuously, and you should never ask a human to do what a machine does better) and because it happens too late (after development), so developers should write automated tests as part of development for immediate feedback and to deliver software rapidly and safely.

Automated testing is essential not only for a short lead time but because it forces you to build a testable application; since it is very hard to add automated testing to an already large, complex application, failing to write automated tests is the fast track to monolithic hell.

The microservice architecture improves testability but its complexity demands automated tests, and a key challenge is verifying that services interact correctly while minimizing the number of slow, complex, and unreliable end-to-end tests that must launch many services.
The developer workflow should be edit code, run fast tests (ideally with a single keystroke), and repeat, so the tests give feedback within seconds.

A test verifies the behavior of the System Under Test (SUT), which may be anything from a single class to the entire application, where a test case is a set of inputs, execution conditions, and expected results developed for a specific objective.

An automated test has four phases: setup (initialize the test fixture, the SUT and its dependencies, to the desired state), exercise (invoke the SUT), verify (make assertions about the outcome and the SUT's state), and teardown (clean up the fixture).

Test a system under test in isolation by replacing its dependencies with test doubles, which makes tests simpler and faster; the two kinds are a stub (returns values to the SUT) and a mock (used to verify the SUT correctly invokes a dependency, and often also a stub).

There are four types of functional test distinguished by scope: unit tests (a small part such as a class), integration tests (a service interacting with infrastructure and other services), component tests (acceptance tests for one service), and end-to-end tests (acceptance tests for the whole application).

Follow the test pyramid: write many fast, simple, reliable unit tests at the base and very few slow, complex, brittle end-to-end tests at the top, because as scope grows tests become slower and less reliable and an unreliable test is almost as bad as no test.

In a microservice architecture the complexity of testing shifts from individual services to the interactions between them, so it is essential to write tests that verify a service interacts correctly with its dependencies and clients.

Each interaction between two services is a contract (over message or event structure and channel, or over a REST endpoint), so a service developer must be confident its dependencies have stable APIs and must avoid unintentionally making breaking changes to its own API.

Do not verify service interactions by running both services end-to-end, because that is slow, pulls in transitive dependencies, and may exercise unrelated business logic; instead use consumer-driven contract testing to test the services in isolation.

A consumer-driven contract test is an integration test for a provider that verifies its API matches a consumer's expectations (the API's shape: HTTP method/path, headers, request/response body and status) rather than the provider's business logic; the consumer team writes the contract test suite and contributes it to the provider's deployment pipeline, so a failure signals a breaking API change.

Consumer-driven contract testing uses testing by example (contracts are concrete example messages), which is more useful for tests than schemas alone because a test still needs an example request to invoke the provider, and it tests both sides: the provider test invokes with the contract's request and checks the response, while the consumer-side test uses the contract to configure a stub so the consumer is tested without running the provider.

Write consumer contract tests for messaging APIs too: a domain-event contract is an example event (the provider emits and verifies it, the consumer verifies it can handle it), and an asynchronous request/response contract pairs a request and response message (the provider verifies its reply, the consumer configures a stub subscriber).

Every service has a deployment pipeline, the automated process of getting code from a developer's desktop into production as a series of stages that run increasingly thorough test suites in increasingly production-like environments, ideally fully automated (often via a CI server) and designed to surface failures as fast as possible.

Order the deployment pipeline fast-feedback-first: pre-commit tests (unit tests, run before committing), a commit stage (compile plus unit tests plus static analysis), integration tests, component tests, then deploy, with each later stage slower and more production-like.
Prefer a unit test over running the whole service to verify a small unit (such as calculating an order subtotal), because a full-service test is more complex and slow.

There are two kinds of unit test: a solitary unit test (tests a class in isolation using mocks or stubs for its dependencies) and a sociable unit test (tests a class together with its real dependencies); the class's role decides which, with controllers and service classes typically using solitary tests and domain objects such as entities and value objects typically using sociable tests.

Choose the unit-test type by class role: test entities, value objects, and sagas with sociable unit tests (they carry the bulk of the business logic together with their dependencies), and test domain services, controllers, and inbound/outbound message gateways with solitary unit tests that mock their dependencies.
Value objects are easy to unit test because they are immutable and have no side effects: create one in a given state, invoke a method, and assert on the return value.

Test a saga with a fast sociable unit test that mocks the database and messaging infrastructure and verifies the saga sends the expected sequence of command messages, covering both the happy path and each rollback scenario triggered by a participant's failure reply, rather than a slow test using a real database and broker with stub participants.

Test a domain service with a mostly-solitary unit test that mocks its repositories and messaging dependencies and then verifies both the returned value and that the dependencies were invoked correctly.

Test a controller with a mock-MVC framework (such as Spring Mock Mvc) that issues mock HTTP requests and asserts on HTTP responses, so it exercises request routing and Java-to-JSON conversion without real network calls, which is more effective than directly instantiating the controller.

Test message and event handler adapters like controllers: instantiate the adapter with a mocked service, publish a message or event to a stubbed messaging infrastructure (no real broker), and verify the adapter invoked the service correctly.

Unit tests thoroughly test business logic and run in seconds (usable as compile-time tests) but do not verify that a service interacts correctly with infrastructure or other services (such as persisting to the database, sending correctly formatted messages on the right channel, or matching another service's event structure), which requires integration tests plus component tests of the whole service in isolation.

Integration tests verify a service interacts correctly with infrastructure and other services without launching services (unlike end-to-end tests), using two simplifying strategies: test each adapter and its supporting classes individually rather than the whole service, and use contracts for interactions with other application services.

A contract is a concrete example of an interaction between a pair of services whose structure depends on the interaction style: an HTTP request and response for REST, a domain event for publish/subscribe, and a command message plus reply message for asynchronous request/response.

Component tests are acceptance tests that test a whole service in isolation using stubs for its dependencies, whereas end-to-end tests test a group of services or the entire application and should be used sparingly because they sit at the top of the test pyramid.

Use each contract to test both sides of an interaction: the consumer-side integration test uses the contract to configure a stub that simulates the provider (so the consumer's adapter is tested without a running provider), and the provider-side test uses the contract to test the provider's adapter with mocks for its dependencies, which ensures both sides agree on the API.

Write persistence integration tests that verify a service's database-access logic (e.g. its JPA repositories) works, because unit tests only exercise in-memory objects; each such test sets up the schema and known state, performs a database operation, asserts on the resulting database and object state, and optionally tears down.
Provision the real database for persistence integration tests by running an instance in Docker rather than mocking it, so the tests exercise the actual database access.

Test REST interservice interactions with consumer-driven contracts: the consumer-side integration test configures an HTTP stub server (such as WireMock) from the contract to simulate the provider, while the provider-side test (code-generated from the contract) exercises the controller with a mock-MVC framework, so each side is verified against the same contract without an end-to-end test.

Test publish/subscribe interactions with contracts that each specify a domain event: the provider-side test triggers the publisher and verifies the emitted event matches the contract, and the consumer-side test publishes the contract's event and verifies the consumer's handler invokes its dependencies correctly.

Test asynchronous request/response interactions with contracts that pair an input (command) message and an output (reply) message: the provider-side test sends the input and verifies the reply matches the contract, and the consumer-side test verifies its command proxy sends correctly structured commands and correctly processes the contract's reply.

Integration and unit tests each verify only individual parts of a service and neither runs the whole service, so verifying that a service works as a whole requires moving up the pyramid to component tests.

The Service Component Test pattern is an acceptance test that treats a service as a black box and verifies its behavior through its API in isolation, replacing the service's dependencies with stubs and possibly in-memory infrastructure, which is far easier and faster than deploying the service with all its transitive dependencies as an end-to-end test.

Acceptance tests are business-facing tests that describe a component's desired externally visible behavior from its clients' perspective rather than its internal implementation, are derived from user stories or use cases, and follow a given-when-then structure mapping to the setup, execute, and verify phases.

Write acceptance tests as executable specifications (for example Gherkin scenarios run by Cucumber) rather than hand-translating scenarios into code, to avoid the scenarios and tests diverging and the ambiguity of manual translation.

Component tests come in two strategies that trade realism against speed: in-process tests run the service in the test's JVM with in-memory stubs, mocks, and database (simpler and faster but not testing the deployable artifact), and out-of-process tests package the service in production format (e.g. a Docker image) and run it as a separate process against real infrastructure (e.g. MySQL and Kafka) while stubbing application-service dependencies (better coverage and closer to deployment but more complex, slower, and more brittle).

In an out-of-process component test, stub the application-service dependencies that send back responses, either by reusing contracts (heavier, and such contracts are often component-test-only) or by configuring stubs from within the test itself (e.g. WireMock for HTTP and messaging stubs for asynchronous interactions), the latter being simpler for interactions involving dynamically generated values.

End-to-end tests are slow, brittle, and time-consuming because they deploy many services and infrastructure (any one of which may fail to deploy), so minimize them and write user-journey tests that exercise a whole slice of functionality in one test (e.g. create, revise, and cancel in a single test) to reduce the number of tests and execution time.
Write end-to-end and acceptance tests in a high-level, business-readable DSL such as Gherkin executed by Cucumber, so business people can understand them.
A production-ready service must satisfy three quality attributes beyond its functional requirements: security, configurability, and observability.

Most security concerns (physical security, encrypting data in transit and at rest, authentication, authorization, and patching) are the same for microservices as for a monolith, but the microservice architecture forces some application-level security to be done differently, notably a mechanism to pass user identity from one service to another.

An application developer is responsible for four security aspects: authentication (verifying the principal's identity from credentials), authorization (verifying the principal may perform the operation on the data, via role-based security and/or access control lists), auditing (tracking a principal's operations for detection, support, and compliance), and secure interprocess communication (ideally all service traffic over TLS, possibly with authentication).
Use a proven security framework (such as Spring Security, Apache Shiro, or Passport) rather than implementing authentication and authorization yourself, because getting them right is challenging.

A monolith typically stores the security context (the principal's id and roles) in an in-memory, thread-local session identified by an opaque session token cookie, but an in-memory session requires sticky routing of a session to one instance (complicating load balancing and session draining), which can be avoided by storing the session in a database or eliminating the server-side session entirely (credentials per request, or session state carried in the token).

A monolith's in-memory security context (thread-local) and centralized in-memory session are nonstarters for a microservice architecture, because services cannot share memory to pass identity and a shared session database would violate loose coupling, so a different identity-passing and session mechanism is required.

Do not authenticate in the individual services, because that lets unauthenticated requests into the internal network, relies on every team implementing security correctly (risking vulnerabilities), and forces each service to handle a diverse set of client authentication mechanisms.

Authenticate each request at the API gateway before forwarding it to the services, so there is only one place to get security right (a smaller vulnerability surface) and only the gateway must handle the diverse authentication mechanisms, hiding that complexity from the services.

Apply the Access Token pattern: after the API gateway authenticates a request it passes a token containing the user's identity and roles to each invoked service, which validates the token and obtains the principal, and the gateway may reuse the same token as the session token for login-based clients.

Authorization can be centralized in the API gateway for role-based access to URL paths (reducing vulnerabilities), but the gateway cannot practically enforce ACLs on individual domain objects (which needs a service's domain knowledge) and doing so risks coupling the gateway to the services, so implement role-based and ACL-based authorization for aggregates within the services.

Prefer transparent tokens such as JWT over opaque tokens (UUIDs) to pass user identity and roles between the gateway and services, because an opaque token forces the recipient to make a synchronous RPC to a security service to validate it and fetch the user (reducing performance and availability and adding latency), whereas a JWT carries the signed claims so no such call is needed.

A JWT securely represents claims (identity, roles, expiry) between two parties and is signed with a secret so a third party cannot forge or tamper with it, but because it is self-contained it is irrevocable, so issue short-lived JWTs to limit a stolen token's damage at the cost of continually reissuing them.

Use an off-the-shelf OAuth 2.0 authorization server or framework rather than building your own security infrastructure, since that functionality is generic; OAuth 2.0 defines an Authorization Server, an Access Token, a Refresh Token (long-lived but revocable, used to obtain a new access token), a Resource Server (the services), and a Client (the API gateway).

Regardless of the specific mechanism, the three key security ideas in a microservice architecture are that the API gateway authenticates clients, the gateway and services use a transparent token such as a JWT to pass principal information, and each service uses the token to obtain the principal's identity and roles.

Do not hard-wire environment-specific configuration into a service (which would force a rebuild per environment) or bake multiple config sets into source code selected by a profile mechanism (a security and deployability risk); build the service once, deploy it to multiple environments, and supply configuration at runtime via the Externalized Configuration pattern, storing secrets in a secrets manager such as Vault or AWS Parameter Store.

Externalized configuration has two models: a push model where the deployment infrastructure supplies configuration to the instance at startup (via environment variables or a configuration file) and a pull model where the instance reads its configuration from a configuration server at startup.

Push-based configuration is effective and widely used but reconfiguring a running service may be impossible (e.g. you cannot change a running process's environment variables) and configuration values risk being scattered across many service definitions.

A configuration server (pull model) provides centralized configuration (one place, with global defaults overridable per service), transparent decryption of sensitive data, and dynamic reconfiguration, at the cost of being another piece of infrastructure to run (mitigated by frameworks such as Spring Cloud Config).

A production application needs observability so operators can see what it is doing, be alerted to problems before users are impacted, and troubleshoot to the root cause, which is harder in a distributed system where a single request spans the API gateway and multiple services.

Design a service to be observable using six patterns, each with a developer component (make the service expose the information) and an operations component (the infrastructure that collects it): Health check API, Log aggregation, Distributed tracing, Exception tracking, Application metrics, and Audit logging.

Apply the Health check API pattern: a service exposes a health endpoint (e.g. GET /health) that the deployment infrastructure invokes periodically to decide whether to route traffic and whether to terminate and replace a failed-but-still-running instance, with the handler typically testing the service's connections to its infrastructure dependencies (e.g. a test database query) and returning a healthy or unhealthy status.

A running service instance may be unable to handle requests (still initializing, or failed without terminating such as exhausting its database connections), so a health check lets the infrastructure avoid routing to a not-ready or failed instance and terminate one that does not recover.

Apply the Log aggregation pattern: aggregate all services' logs into a centralized database that supports searching and alerting, because in a microservice architecture the log entries for a single request are scattered across the gateway and multiple services.

In modern deployment environments (containers, serverless, some of which such as AWS Lambda have no permanent filesystem), have a service log to stdout rather than to a filesystem log file and let the deployment infrastructure decide what to do with the output.

Log aggregation infrastructure (for example the ELK stack: an Elasticsearch store, a Logstash pipeline, and Kibana visualization) ships each service instance's logs to a centralized logging server for viewing, searching, and alerting, with the pipeline and server being an operations responsibility while developers must write services that generate useful logs.

Apply the Distributed tracing pattern: assign each external request a unique id and record how it flows from service to service (with start and end times) in a centralized server for visualization and analysis, where a trace represents one external request and consists of spans (each span an operation with a name and start/end time, and possibly child spans for nested operations).

Distributed tracing works via an instrumentation library in each service (which manages traces and spans, propagates trace state on outbound requests through headers such as the B3 standard, and reports spans) plus a distributed-tracing server (such as Zipkin) that stitches spans into traces and stores and visualizes them.

Integrate distributed tracing through interceptors or aspect-oriented programming (for example Spring Cloud Sleuth) rather than calling the instrumentation library directly from service code, to keep the instrumentation logic from intertwining with business logic.

A valuable side effect of distributed tracing is a unique request id that a service can include in its log entries, so that combined with log aggregation you can find all log entries for a single external request.

Apply the Application metrics pattern: services report metrics to a central server that aggregates, visualizes, and alerts, where a metric sample has a name, a numeric value, and a timestamp plus optional dimensions (name-value pairs such as machine, service, or instance) that the system aggregates along.

A service developer is responsible for two metrics tasks: instrumenting the service to collect metrics about its behavior (e.g. counters for orders placed, approved, and rejected) and exposing those metrics, along with JVM and framework metrics, to the metrics server.
Deliver metrics to the metrics service either by push (the instance sends metrics via an API, e.g. AWS CloudWatch) or by pull (the metrics service scrapes a service endpoint, e.g. Prometheus).

Apply the Exception tracking pattern: report exceptions to a central service that de-duplicates them, generates alerts, and manages their resolution, which is better than scraping logs (logs are line-oriented rather than multi-line, offer no resolution tracking, and do not de-duplicate); integrate via the tracker's client library (e.g. a servlet filter) rather than calling its API directly.

Apply the Audit logging pattern: record each user's action (their identity, the action, and the business objects involved) in a database to help customer support, ensure compliance, and detect suspicious behavior.

Implement audit logging in one of three ways: add logging code to the business logic (simple but it intertwines concerns and is error-prone), use AOP advice to automatically record each service-method call (reliable but the advice sees only the method name and arguments, making business context hard to capture), or use event sourcing (which gives an automatic audit log for create/update operations with the user id in each event but does not record queries).

Apply the Microservice chassis pattern: build services on a framework or set of frameworks that handle cross-cutting concerns (externalized configuration, health checks, application metrics, service discovery, circuit breakers, distributed tracing, logging, exception tracking) so you write little or no code for them and can focus on business logic.

A drawback of a microservice chassis is that you need one for each language/platform combination, and over time many of its functions migrate to the infrastructure (e.g. service discovery) or to a service mesh.

Apply the Service mesh pattern: route all network traffic in and out of services through a networking layer that implements circuit breakers, distributed tracing, service discovery, load balancing, rule-based traffic routing, and TLS-secured interprocess communication, which moves those concerns out of the services (shrinking the chassis to app-tightly-coupled concerns like configuration and health checks plus propagating tracing headers) and works across languages.

A service mesh's traffic-routing ability lets you separate deployment from release: deploy a new version of a service into production but release it only to certain users, such as internal test users.

Deployment combines two concepts, the process (the steps people take to get software into production) and the architecture (the structure of the runtime environment); DevOps makes the development team responsible for deploying, ideally through an automated deployment pipeline.

Treat production machines as immutable, disposable cattle (discarded and recreated) rather than hand-tended pets (reconfigured in place), because at microservice scale (tens or hundreds of services) hand-configuring servers is impractical and a highly automated deployment process and infrastructure is required.

A production environment must provide four capabilities: a service-management interface to create, update, and configure services (ideally a REST API), runtime service management that keeps the desired number of instances running (restarting crashed instances and rescheduling them off failed machines), monitoring (logs and metrics plus alerting), and request routing from users to services.
There are four deployment options for a service: deploy as a language-specific package, deploy as a virtual machine, deploy as a container, and serverless deployment.

The Language-specific packaging format pattern deploys the service's language-specific package (a JAR/WAR, a directory of source and modules, or an OS-specific executable) onto a machine that has the runtime installed; its benefits are fast deployment and efficient resource use (especially running multiple instances per machine or process), and a service instance is typically a single process (sometimes a group).

The language-specific packaging pattern's drawbacks are that it does not encapsulate the technology stack (operations must know each service's exact runtime versions, which is error-prone), cannot constrain a service instance's resources (a bug can starve others of CPU or memory), gives no isolation between co-located instances (a misbehaving one impacts the others), and makes automatic instance placement hard, so it should rarely be used except when efficiency outweighs all other concerns.

The Deploy a service as a VM pattern packages each service as a VM image (e.g. an AWS AMI) built by the deployment pipeline so that each instance is a VM, typically managed by an auto-scaling group that keeps the desired number of healthy instances running.

Deploying services as VMs benefits from the VM image encapsulating the whole technology stack (a deployable black box that avoids error-prone software installation and can be deployed anywhere via the VM management API), complete resource isolation per instance, and mature, highly automated cloud infrastructure (scheduling, load balancing, autoscaling).

Deploying services as VMs has drawbacks: less efficient resource use (each instance carries a full OS and coarse VM sizes cause underutilization, worse for lightweight NodeJS/Go services), relatively slow deployments (large image build and instantiation plus OS boot take minutes), and system-administration overhead of patching the OS and runtime.

The Deploy a service as a container pattern uses operating-system-level virtualization: one or a few processes run in an isolated sandbox with their own IP address (so no port conflicts) and root filesystem while sharing the host OS, and you specify each container's CPU/memory/IO so the runtime enforces the limits, which is essential for an orchestrator to place containers without overloading machines.

Deploy a container by building an image from a Dockerfile (a base image plus install/config steps, a startup command, and ideally a HEALTHCHECK), pushing it to a registry, and running containers from it; a Docker image's layered filesystem transfers quickly because only the changed application layers move over the network.

The docker run command alone is not a reliable production deployment because it runs a container on a single machine (Docker restarts crashed containers but does not handle machine crashes) and does not deploy a service with its dependencies as a unit; Docker Compose declares a set of containers in YAML to start and stop as a group but is limited to one machine, so reliable production deployment requires a Docker orchestration framework such as Kubernetes.

Deploying services as containers keeps the VM-like benefits (tech-stack encapsulation through the container API, instance isolation, and constrained resources) while being lightweight (fast image builds, fast layered network transfer, and near-instant start with no OS boot), but you must still patch the OS and runtime and administer the container and VM infrastructure unless using a hosted container solution.

A Docker orchestration framework such as Kubernetes treats a set of Docker machines as a single resource pool and provides three functions: resource management (the cluster as a pool of CPU, memory, and storage), scheduling (selecting a node by the container's resource needs and node availability, with affinity and anti-affinity), and service management (named, versioned services kept at the desired healthy instance count, load-balanced, with rolling upgrades and rollback).

A Kubernetes cluster consists of one or more masters (running the API server, the etcd key-value store, the scheduler, and a controller manager whose replication controller keeps the desired instance count running) and nodes (each running a Kubelet that manages pods and a kube-proxy for networking and load balancing), where a pod, the unit of deployment, is a set of containers.

The key Kubernetes objects for a developer are the Pod (the basic deployment unit, one or more containers sharing an IP and storage, ephemeral, optionally with sidecar containers), the Deployment (a declarative controller that keeps the desired number of pod instances running with rolling upgrades and rollbacks, one per microservice), the Service (a stable IP and DNS endpoint that load-balances across pods, i.e. infrastructure-provided service discovery), and the ConfigMap (name-value externalized configuration, with a Secret variant for sensitive values).

Configure two Kubernetes health probes on a service: a readinessProbe that decides whether to route traffic to an instance and a livenessProbe that decides whether to terminate and restart an instance, so Kubernetes routes only to ready instances and restarts failed ones.
Store sensitive configuration such as database passwords in a Kubernetes Secret rather than a plain ConfigMap or literal environment value.

Expose a service outside the Kubernetes cluster with a NodePort service (a cluster-wide port on every node, load-balanced to the pods, which you can front with your own load balancer for full control) or a LoadBalancer service (which auto-provisions a cloud load balancer but gives less configuration control), since the default ClusterIP service is reachable only inside the cluster.

Kubernetes performs a zero-downtime rolling upgrade by incrementally creating new-version pods and terminating old pods only once their replacements are ready (using the readinessProbe), so requests are always served; if the new pods fail to start the deployment gets stuck and you either fix the YAML or roll back with kubectl rollout undo.

A rolling upgrade alone does not prevent a bug that only surfaces under production traffic from impacting users, so separate deployment (getting a service running in production) from release (making it available to end users).

Testing a new version only in a staging environment is unreliable because staging is not an exact clone of production (it is smaller, handles less traffic, and is hard to keep synchronized), so some bugs appear only in production.

Roll out a new version reliably by deploying it to production without routing user traffic to it, testing it in production, then incrementally releasing it to a growing fraction of users (reverting on any issue), ideally through an automated pipeline that monitors the new version for errors.

A service mesh makes separating deployment from release far easier through rule-based traffic routing that can safely run multiple versions of a service simultaneously (for example routing test users to a new version while end users stay on the old one).

A service mesh such as Istio has a control plane that implements management and configuration (e.g. Istio's Pilot and Mixer) and a data plane of per-instance proxies (Envoy sidecars) through which all service traffic flows, with features spanning traffic management, security (TLS), telemetry (metrics and distributed tracing), and policy enforcement (quotas and rate limits).

Apply the Sidecar pattern: implement cross-cutting concerns in a sidecar process or container that runs alongside the service instance (for example a service mesh's Envoy proxy running in the service's pod).

Control service-mesh routing declaratively (e.g. an Istio VirtualService defines how to route requests for a host and a DestinationRule defines named subsets of pods, typically service versions, plus traffic policies), which lets you deploy a new version with zero traffic and then route matched requests (such as those with a test-user header) to it before shifting production traffic.

Roll out with a canary release: after testing a new version in production, route only a small percentage of production traffic to it (e.g. 5%) and incrementally increase to 100% as confidence grows, using weighted traffic routing (e.g. a service mesh).

The Serverless deployment pattern (e.g. AWS Lambda) deploys a service as stateless functions that the public cloud runs on demand, so there are no pre-provisioned or idle VMs/containers to pay for and no operating system or runtime to administer.

A lambda function is a stateless service that is packaged (as a ZIP or JAR) and uploaded, after which the platform automatically runs enough instances to handle the load and bills per request by the time taken and memory consumed.

A lambda function can be invoked in four ways: by an HTTP request (via an API gateway acting as an HTTP proxy), by an event generated by a cloud service (e.g. an S3 object, a DynamoDB change, or a Kinesis message), by a cron-like schedule, and by a direct web-service API call (synchronous or asynchronous).

Serverless deployment's benefits are deep integration with cloud services, elimination of system administration (no OS or runtime patching), elasticity (the platform auto-scales to load with no capacity prediction or over/under-provisioning), and usage-based pricing (charged only for the resources consumed per request).

Serverless deployment's drawbacks are long-tail latency from cold-start provisioning (worse for slow-starting services like Java, so poor for latency-sensitive services) and a limited event/request-based programming model unsuited to long-running services (such as consuming from a message broker), so evaluate whether serverless fits a service's requirements before considering alternatives.

Choose the most lightweight deployment pattern that supports a service's requirements, evaluating in order serverless, containers (with an orchestrator such as Kubernetes), virtual machines, and language-specific packages (generally avoiding the last unless you have only a few services); containers are more flexible with more predictable latency than serverless, and VMs can be easier than setting up an orchestrator for a small, simple application.
A team can escape monolithic hell by incrementally converting the monolith to microservices rather than rewriting the application from scratch.

Refactor a monolith to microservices with the Strangler Application pattern: incrementally build a new application of services around the legacy monolith by implementing new features as services and extracting services, so the monolith shrinks over time until it disappears or becomes just another microservice, delivering value early and often unlike a big-bang rewrite.

Only migrate to microservices to solve a significant business problem (such as slow delivery, buggy releases, or poor scalability), because the refactoring diverts resources from feature development and needs the business's support.

Before migrating, confirm the problems come from outgrowing the architecture rather than from a poor development process (e.g. manual testing) or a separately solvable scalability issue: try simpler solutions first and migrate only if delivery problems persist.

Do not do a big-bang rewrite (building the new application from scratch), because it is extremely risky, spends months or years merely duplicating existing functionality against a constantly moving target, and may reimplement features that are no longer needed.

Demonstrate value early and often by refactoring the high-value, constantly evolving areas of the application first (each new service using a modern stack and DevOps process to raise velocity), which maintains the business's support for the migration effort.

Avoid widespread changes to the monolith during migration because they are time-consuming, costly, and risky, and use strategies that reduce the impact (such as replicating an extracted service's data back to the monolith and carefully sequencing extractions).

Make only a minimal up-front investment in deployment infrastructure when starting a microservice migration; the one thing you cannot live without is a deployment pipeline with automated testing, and you should defer sophisticated deployment, discovery, and observability technology (a hard-coded config file for discovery suffices early) until you have a few services and real experience.

There are three strategies to strangle the monolith: implement new features as services (which stops the monolith growing and quickly shows value), separate the presentation tier from the backend, and extract business capabilities into services (which is how functionality is actually migrated and which you will definitely use).

Do not add new features to an unmanageable monolith (stop digging); implement them as services, which reduces the monolith's growth rate, speeds development in a fresh code base, and quickly demonstrates the value of microservices.

Integrate a new service with the monolith using an API gateway (routing new-feature requests to the service and legacy requests to the monolith) and integration glue code (adapters in both the service and the monolith using IPC such as REST and domain events that let the service access the monolith's data and functionality).

Not every new feature can be a service (some are too small to be meaningful or too tightly coupled to the monolith, causing excessive interprocess communication or data-consistency problems); implement such a feature in the monolith initially and extract it later along with related features.

Split the presentation tier from the business and data-access tiers along the business tier's coarse-grained facade API, which lets the two be developed, deployed, and scaled independently (enabling rapid UI iteration and A/B testing) and exposes a remote API for future services, though it is only a partial solution because a resulting application usually remains an unmanageable monolith.

Extract a business capability as a vertical slice (its inbound adapters, domain logic, outbound adapters, and database schema) into a standalone service, with the API gateway routing to it and integration glue connecting it to the monolith, and extract the parts that are high-value and constantly evolving, asking what the benefit is before extracting.

When splitting a domain model to extract a service, eliminate object references that would span service boundaries (a service instance is a separate process) by treating the classes as DDD aggregates and replacing an object reference with the referenced aggregate's primary key.

Extracting a service also moves data: move its tables from the monolith's database to the service's database, and when you split an entity, apply the Split Table refactoring to split its table and move the new table to the service.

Reduce widespread changes to the monolith when extracting a service by replicating the extracted service's data back to the monolith's database for a transition period, making the moved fields read-only and keeping them up to date by replication, so that you only need to change the places in the monolith that update those fields.

Replacing an object reference with a primary key is a minor change to a class but can have a large impact on the class's clients (which expect an object reference), so reduce the impact by having the service define a local replica of the referenced class.

Start a microservice migration with a short time-boxed (e.g. a couple of weeks) architecture-definition effort that defines a target set of services as a destination, but treat that architecture as revisable as you learn from breaking apart the monolith.

Choose an extraction sequence with one of two strategies: freeze monolith development and extract services on demand (which forces the breakup but is driven by short-term needs and risks much work for little benefit) or a planned approach that ranks modules by expected benefit (accelerating development of high-change areas, solving a performance/scaling/reliability problem, or enabling another extraction) and adds ranked refactoring tasks to the backlog; the planned approach is more strategic and aligned with the business.
Extracting a service invariably splits what were originally ACID transactions, so you must ensure data consistency is still maintained between the service and the monolith, sometimes using sagas.

Design the integration glue's API by interaction type: expose a repository interface when a party queries data owned by the other and a service interface when a party invokes an operation on the other, so the business logic need not know the underlying IPC mechanism.

For a cross-party query, either invoke the provider's query API (simple but potentially inefficient with many requests or large responses, and reducing availability because it is synchronous IPC) or maintain a replica (a CQRS view kept current by subscribing to the provider's domain events, which gives efficient queries but is complex to maintain and may require modifying the monolith to publish events).

For a cross-party update, maintain data consistency by communicating via transactional messaging: in a simple case trigger the update with a notification message or event, and in a complex case use a saga.

Implement an Anti-Corruption Layer between a new service's clean domain model and the legacy monolith's model: a translation layer (in repositories, service adapters, and event handlers on both the service and monolith sides) that prevents one domain model's concepts from polluting the other.

A monolith can publish domain events either by inserting event-publishing calls wherever an entity changes (hard to locate all sites, error-prone, and impossible for stored-procedure logic) or at the database level via transaction log tailing or polling (which does not require changing the monolith but tends to publish table-change events rather than high-level business events).

Sagas that extract a service are much easier to implement when the monolith's transactions are only pivot or retriable transactions (never compensatable), because a compensatable monolith transaction needs a semantic-lock state (e.g. APPROVAL_PENDING) that can require widespread, risky changes; therefore carefully order service extractions so the monolith never needs to execute a compensating transaction.

Design an extraction saga so the monolith's transaction is the pivot transaction (the saga's go/no-go point) with the compensatable transactions residing in the new, more-testable service, so the monolith never has to roll back and needs only minimal change.

Sequence service extractions so the monolith's transactions are always pivot or retriable (never compensatable) transactions, which avoids widespread and risky changes to the hard-to-test monolith; for example, extracting Order Service and Consumer Service first can make later extractions leave the monolith's transaction as a pivot.

Support the monolith's session-based security and JWT-based microservice security simultaneously during migration with one small change to the monolith's login handler: return an extra cookie carrying a JWT with the user's id and roles, which the API gateway validates and maps to the Authorization header when it invokes a service, giving every service the user identity in a standard, client-independent way and letting you defer extracting user management.

A service that implements a new feature usually still accesses data owned by the monolith, so it needs integration glue such as a repository proxy that calls the monolith's REST query API and event subscribers that replicate the monolith's entities.

Choose the cross-service query mechanism by cost: use the monolith's query API for data needed rarely and in small amounts (e.g. customer contact info) but maintain a replica updated by subscribing to the monolith's events for data queried often or in bulk (e.g. open orders and restaurant hours), where the replica need only store the subset of attributes the service uses.

Extract a service by identifying the entities and fields that implement the target capability (noting which are also used by the monolith), deciding which data to move (owning the fields the service is responsible for while leaving shared fields in the monolith to minimize change), and copying and stripping the domain logic from the monolith (breaking its dependencies, which is easier in a statically typed language).

To minimize change, an initially extracted service can expose no publicly accessible API and be invoked only by the monolith, extracting just the core algorithm while leaving related operations in the monolith.

Prefer a notification-based API (the caller explicitly tells the service to perform an operation via typed notification messages carrying the needed data) over having the service subscribe to the caller's domain events, so the service stays focused on its own concern and needs no knowledge of the caller's entity lifecycle.

Let the monolith read data that was moved into an extracted service by replicating that data from the service back to the monolith (the service publishes domain events and the monolith consumes them to update its database), which leaves the monolith's schema unchanged and avoids extensive monolith changes.

Encapsulate access to an extracted capability behind a coarse-grained, remotable interface (matching the messaging API), implemented initially by a local class that calls the existing in-monolith code and later by a proxy that sends messages to the standalone service.

Refactoring the monolith to invoke an extracted capability through its new interface at every call site is one of the most challenging parts of extraction, and is easier when the monolith is written in a statically typed language (tools identify the dependencies) or has good automated test coverage.

Roll out an extracted service behind a feature toggle: implement the interface with a toggle-controlled class that switches between the old in-monolith implementation and the new service, so you can deploy and test the service, flip traffic to it, and switch back if it misbehaves, which decouples deploying code from releasing it and reduces rollout risk.
